events.event_narrative: The extreme cold wind chills extended into January 1, 2022.

Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were common across the county with heavier amounts in eastern reaches that received the edge of the lake-effect snow. The highest total was 18 inches at Lake Nebagamon.

Snowfall totals varied greatly from south to north across the county with around 3 to 5 inches in southern areas to nearly two feet along the Bayfield Peninsula. One station just northwest of the city of Bayfield received 23 inches of snow from the system and the lake-effect snow on the backside.

Snowfall amounts varied greatly across the county depending on where the lake-effect snow bands that developed as the system departed set up. Totals ranged from around 7 inches to around 16 inches with Mellen receiving 22.5 inches total after an extended time under a snow band.

Snowfall totals of 7 to 12 inches were common across the county with the Gile area receiving 21.5 inches of snow by the time the snow ended after being under a lake-effect snow band for an extended period of time.
An area of heavier than expected snowfall moved across Price County leading to totals of 6 to 9 inches across much of the area. The highest report was 11.5 inches near Butternut.
Most of the snowfall totals in the area were under 6 inches, but a localized area of heavy snowfall northwest of Duluth near Payne led to a few reports just over 6 inches in that area.
Snowfall totals were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range across southern Lake County, but a few reports to around 6 inches were received from the Two Harbors area.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 6 inches were common across southern Cook County with higher amounts around 8 inches reported in the Lutsen and Tofte areas.

Most of the snowfall totals in the area were under 6 inches, but a localized area of heavy snowfall northwest of Duluth near Culver and areas along the North Shore received 6 to 7 inches of accumulation. The highest total was 7.5 inches near Culver.

Snowfall totals adjacent to Lake Superior in southern Lake County were in the 3 to 6 inch range with a few reports over 6 inches near the Lake/Cook border. The highest report was 6.8 inches 3 miles north-northeast of Finland.

Snowfall totals of 7 to 9 inches were received within roughly 5 miles of Lake Superior along the North Shore in Cook County. The highest report was from 10 miles northeast of Grand Marias where 9.5 inches was recorded.

Most of the county was in the D2 Severe Drought category with a sliver of D1 Moderate Drought across the far eastern portion of the county. Generally near normal precipitation was received over the course of the month and no change in the drought status was observed.

The far northwestern corner of northern Itasca County remained in D2 Severe Drought throughout the month with D1 Moderate Drought in place across the balance of northern Itasca County. Precipitation for the month was near to slightly below normal, but no change in the drought status was observed.

Much of northern Lake and Cook counties remained under D2 Severe Drought throughout January with just far western Lake County being in D1 Moderate Drought. Precipitation for the month was within a few tenths of an inch of normal with portions of eastern Cook County receiving up to a half of an inch of precipitation above normal. Precipitation at the end of December led to the trimming of the area of D2 Severe Drought across southeastern Lake County with the update on the 11th, but no further changes were observed over the remainder of the month.

The eastern half of southern Lake County remained under D2 Severe Drought to begin January with the western portion being in D1 Moderate Drought. Precipitation for the month was within a few tenths of an inch of normal and precipitation at the end of December and beginning of January led to the removal of the area of D2 Severe Drought across southern Lake County with the update on the 11th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought across the area. No further changes were seen over the remainder of the month.

All of southern Cook County remained under D2 Severe Drought to begin January. Precipitation for the month was within a few tenths of an inch of normal with portions of eastern Cook County receiving up to a half of an inch of precipitation above normal. Precipitation at the end of December and beginning of January led to the trimming of the area of D2 Severe Drought across southwestern Cook County with the update on the 11th, but no further changes were observed over the remainder of the month.

The northeastern corner of Bayfield County remained in D2 Severe Drought to begin the month. Precipitation for the month ended up near to below normal, but a deep snowpack and precipitation at the end of December and beginning of January led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought over the area with the update on the 11th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought conditions across the entirety of the county.

The far northern reaches of Ashland County remained in D2 Severe Drought to begin the month. Precipitation for the month ended up near to below normal, but a deep snowpack and precipitation at the end of December and beginning of January led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought over the area with the update on the 11th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought conditions across the entirety of the county.

The far northern reaches of Iron County remained in D2 Severe Drought to begin the month. Precipitation for the month ended up near to below normal, but a deep snowpack and precipitation at the end of December and beginning of January led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought over the area with the update on the 11th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought conditions across the entirety of the county.
Snowfall totals of 2 to 4 inches were common across the county with locally higher report of 7.8 inches near Silver Bay.
Snowfall totals of 1 to 3 inches were common across the county with locally higher reports of 6 inches near Lutsen.
Snowfall totals of 1 to 4 inches were common across the county with locally higher reports of 6 inches near Twig.
Snowfall totals of 3 to 5 inches were common across the county with locally higher reports of 6 inches near Hovland.
Snowfall totals of 3 to 6 inches were common across the central portion of St. Louis County with a high report of 7.8 inches near Payne.

Snowfall totals of around a foot were received across southern Lake County by the time snowfall ended. The highest report was 14 inches as of 8AM on the 22nd eight miles northeast of Two Harbors, but no additional reports were received from this station after this despite snow continuing for an additional 18 hours.
Snowfall of 6 to 8 inches was received across northern Cass County with this system. The highest report was 9.1 inches 11.5 miles southwest of Remer.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 9 inches were received across the southern part of Itasca County with a high report of 9.1 inches near Coleraine.
Heavier snowfall totals were seen across the southern portion of Cass County where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were received. The highest report was 16 inches just north of Pillager.
Snowfall of 10 to 14 inches was reported across the county with the highest reports coming from the southern half. The highest report was 14.9 inches near Fort Ripley.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were received across northern Aitkin County with the highest report being 10.7 inches near McGregor.
Snowfall reports across the southern half of the county ranged from 10 to 16 inches with 19.8 inches recorded just to the northeast of Isle.

Snowfall totals of 10 to 17 inches were reported across southern St. Louis County with slightly lower amounts in Carlton County. The highest report was 20 inches in southeastern Duluth. The combination of heavy snow and high winds at one point led to closures of both the Bong and Blatnik bridges due to vehicle collisions involving numerous vehicles, however, no injuries were reported with these incidents.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 11 inches were received from Pine County with a high report of 11.2 inches near Sturgeon Lake.

Snowfall totals of 9 to 15 inches were received from across the county with a high report of 15.4 inches near Poplar. The combination of heavy snow and high winds at one point led to closures of both the Bong and Blatnik bridges due to vehicle collisions involving numerous vehicles, however, no injuries were reported with these incidents.

Snowfall was prolific across Bayfield County during the event, especially across the Bayfield Peninsula. Snowfall ranged from around 10 inches in the southern part of the county to over 30 inches in the Bayfield Peninsula. The highest report was 33.5 inches just outside of Washburn and at one point early in the event, snowfall rates of 1 to 3 inches per hour were observed for multiple hours.

Snowfall amounts varied greatly from south to north across the county with around 10 inches in southern areas to as much as 25 inches near Ashland in the northern part of the county. Snowfall was so heavy at one point during the storm, US2 was closed through Ashland where it runs adjacent to Lake Superior for over 12 hours on Tuesday with a detour further inland.
Snowfall of 9 to 12 inches was recorded across Iron County with a high report of 14.5 inches in Gile.
Snowfall of 6 to 12 inches was received across Burnett County with the highest report of 13.8 inches coming from near Danbury.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with fresh snow and falling snow led to a snow squall along Minnesota Highway 371 in western Crow Wing County around noon. The squall moved off Gull Lake and over the roadway leading to near zero visibility. This sudden change in conditions resulted in a chain reaction wreck that involved 23 vehicles, including three semi-trailers. Three people were taken to a local hospital due to injuries sustained in the wreck. The road remained closed for much of the afternoon while cleanup was taking place.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with heavy snowfall moved from west to east across the southern reaches of southern St. Louis County and northern Carlton County during the early afternoon hours. Visibilities rapidly dropped to a quarter of a mile or less with rapid snow accumulations on roadways per webcams in the area. Travel was especially difficult along I-35 from Cloquet to Duluth as the snow squall passed through.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with heavy snowfall moved from west to east across northern Douglas County during the early afternoon hours. Visibilities rapidly dropped to a quarter of a mile or less with rapid snow accumulations on roadways per webcams in the area. Travel was especially difficult along US2 and US53, especially in the Superior area, as the snow squall passed through.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with heavy snowfall moved from west to east across the northern reaches of Bayfield County during the early afternoon hours. Visibilities rapidly dropped to a quarter of a mile or less with rapid snow accumulations on roadways per webcams in the area. Travel was especially difficult along US2 as the snow squall passed through.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with heavy snowfall moved from west to east across the northern half of Ashland County during the mid-afternoon hours. Visibilities rapidly dropped to a quarter of a mile or less with rapid snow accumulations on roadways per webcams in the area. Travel was especially difficult along US2 as the snow squall passed through with visibilities falling to nearly zero on the east side of Ashland per one webcam view.

Snow Squall. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph along with heavy snowfall moved from west to east across the northern half of Iron County during the mid-afternoon hours. Visibilities rapidly dropped to a quarter of a mile or less with rapid snow accumulations on roadways per webcams in the area. Travel was especially difficult along US2 as the snow squall passed through.

Most of the county was in the D2 Severe Drought category with a sliver of D1 Moderate Drought across the far eastern portion of the county. Generally near normal to slightly above normal precipitation was received over the course of the month, but no change in the drought status was observed.

The far northwestern corner of northern Itasca County remained in D2 Severe Drought throughout the month with D1 Moderate Drought in place across the balance of northern Itasca County. Precipitation for the month was near to slightly above normal, but no change in the drought status was observed.

Much of Cook County with the northeastern quarter of Lake County remained under D2 Severe Drought throughout February with the remainder of Lake County being in D1 Moderate Drought. Precipitation for the month was near to slightly above normal, but no change in the drought status was realized by the end of the month.

Much of southern Cook County remained under D2 Severe Drought to begin February with a small area of D1 Moderate Drought in the southwestern corner of the county. Precipitation for the month was near to slightly above normal for the month and this was enough to remove the area of D2 Severe Drought completely from the area with the update on the 22, leaving D1 Moderate Drought across southern Cook County for the remainder of the month.
Snowfall of around 5 followed about a hundreth of an inch of ice accumulation early in the storm near Solon Springs.

Bayfield County had some of the worst impacts from the storm with almost 0.40 of ice acumulation reported near Moquah followed by 7.5 of snow at nearby Bayfield during the latter half of the storm. The nearly 0.40 of ice accumulation fell in a six hour period at the start of the storm.
Ice accumulation of 0.30 inches was reported in Mellen during the storm.
Ice accumulations up to 0.30 inches was reported in the Ironwood area by the time the storm ended.
Ice accumulations of a quarter of an inch were reported near Webster.
Ice accumulations of a quarter of an inch were reported near Shell Lake.

Ice accumulations of a quarter of an inch were reported in a time period of around six to eight hours in the Hayward area at the beginning of the storm. Jump River Electrical Cooperative reported approximately 500 customers without power during the height of the storm due to downed lines from the ice and trees/branches falling onto lines.
International Falls recorded 13.1 inches of snow by the time the storm ended.
Snowfall totals of 6 to just over 7 inches were reported across northern St. Louis County along with freezing rain accumulations of up to 0.20 inches in Ely.
Snowfall totals of 8 to 10 inches were reported across the area with a high report of 10.1 up the hill from Grand Marais. Higher totals were possible across the BWCAW.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were reported across northern Itasca County with a high report of 8.5 inches near Talmoon.

Snowfall totals were generally in the 4 to 6 inch range across the central part of St. Louis County, but areas along the Koochiching and Itasca county borders received a little over 6 inches with the Celina area seeing 7 inches of accumulation.

Snowfall of 3 to 6 inches was received across much of southern Lake County with higher amounts to around 10 inches in the eastern reaches of the county. The highest report was 10.7 inches near Silver Bay.
Heavy snowfall fell across southern Cook County with 10 to 14 inches being common across the area. The highest report was 15.5 inches near Grand Portage.
Snowfall totals across the area were generally under 6 inches, but a few locations did receive slightly over 6 inches including a report of 7 inches near Federal Dam.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 6 inches were reported across the southern reaches of southern Itasca County, but 6 to 8 inches were received in northern areas with 8 inches reported near Deer River.
A heavy burst of snow across northern Itasca County led to reports of 3 to 6 inches across the northern part of the county. A high report of 7.5 inches was recorded near Wirt in about 10 hours.
A period of freezing rain along the North Shore was recorded during the early morning hours of the 30th. A quarter of an inch of ice was reported near Castle Danger in about a 6 to 8 hour period.

Heavier than expected freezing rain was received across the Bayfield Peninsula during the storm due to onshore winds from Lake Superior bringing cooler surface temperatures into the area. A quarter of an inch of ice was recorded near Red Cliff with this storm.

Heavy freezing rain was recorded across parts of Sawyer County with amounts around a quarter of an inch or higher in many areas. The town of Ojibwa received 0.38 inches of ice accumulation by the time freezing rain ended.

Freezing rain decreased from west to east across the county with more rain being received in eastern areas. Around a quarter of an inch of ice was received along the Price/Sawyer County line with the system.

Much of the county began the month with D2 Severe Drought in place with a small area of D1 Moderate Drought in place across the far eastern part of the county. Precipitation was generally near to slightly below normal over the course of the month, but, when combined with winter snow melt, this was enough to recharge the soil and lead to the removal of D2 Severe Drought across the county with the update on the 29th.  This left mainly D1 Moderate Drought in place across the county with an area of D0 Abnormally Dry in far eastern areas.

Much of the northern part of the county began the month with D1 Moderate Drought in place with a small area of D2 Severe Drought in place across the northwestern part of the county. Precipitation was generally near to slightly below normal over the course of the month, but, when combined with winter snow melt, this was enough to recharge the soil and lead to the removal of D2 Severe Drought across the county with the update on the 29th.  This left mainly D0 Abnormally Dry conditions in place across the county with an area of D1 Moderate Dry in the northwestern corner.

Much of northern Cool County began the month with D2 Severe Drought with the northeastern corner of Lake County in D2 Severe Drought. D1 Moderate Drought was in place elsewhere across northern Lake and Cook Counties. Precipitation was generally near to slightly above  normal over the course of the month, and, when combined with winter snow melt, this was enough to recharge the soil and lead to the removal of D2 Severe Drought across the area with the update on the 29th following a slight reduction in area with the update on the 8th.  This left mainly D1 Moderate Drought in place across the county with D0 Abnormally Dry conditions in far southern areas.
Widespread snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were seen across the area with a foot of snow being observed near Murphy City.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were reported near Lake Superior in the southern part of the county through the event with a high total of 13 inches near Silver Bay.
Snowfall of 6 to 9 inches was recorded across the southern part of the county, with most falling on the 6th. A station north of Lutsen received just short of a foot with this system.
Widespread snowfall of 4 to 6 inches was reported across northern Cass County with a few small pockets of 6 to 8 inches near Remer and Cass Lake.
Snowfall totals across Carlton County were in the 2 to 5 inch range. Southeastern St. Louis County saw upwards of 6 to 8 inches near Duluth, with totals quickly falling off to the north and west.
The far northern part of the county received 6 to 8 inches of snow through the event with totals quickly dropping to the south. A 3-day total of nearly 11 inches was reported near Poplar.

Snowfall totals ranged from 4 to 6 inches in the southern part of the county to 6 to 8 inches across the Bayfield Peninsula. One station near the top of the terrain ridge received a total of 8.2 inches from the storm.
The northern third of the county received 6 to 8 inches with snow totals dwindling further to the south.
The northern third of the county received around 6 inches of snowfall with totals dwindling towards the southern part of the county to around 2 inches. A total of 6.8 inches was reported in Gile.
Snowfall reports of 4 to 6 inches were received across the area with a high report of 6.5 inches at Wolf Ridge near Finland.
Snowfall reports of 6 to 7 inches were largely confined to the along the North Shore of Lake Superior with just over 7 inches being reported near Grand Marais.

Snow squall. Wind gusts of 30 to 35 mph and heavy snowfall led to visibilities around 1/2 mile or less in areas along the Gunflint Trail. Webcams showed visibility as low as 1/4 mile or less at times during the heaviest squalls.

Snow squall. Wind gusts of 30 to 35 mph and heavy snowfall led to visibilities around 1/2 mile or less in areas along the Gunflint Trail and along US Highway 61 along the northern Lake Superior shore. Webcams showed visibility as low as 1/4 mile or less at times during the heaviest squalls.
Several pine trees approximately 12 to 14 inches in diameter were snapped near the trunk.
An eight inch diameter tree was downed onto a power line.
A localized area of just over 6 inches of snow fell in the northeast corner of the county. Totals elsewhere across the northern part of the county were around 4 inches or less.
A few trees were reported down in the Spooner area.
A few trees were reported down in the Shell Lake area.
Trees and power lines were downed across western Sawyer County with the majority of reports coming from around Hayward.
A large tree was downed onto Highway 27 to the north of Hayward Hospital.
A few tree limbs around 3 inches in diameter were broken by the storm.
Two 12 inch diameter poplar trees were snapped during the storm.
Many large trees were reported down along with numerous power outages on the Lac Courte Oreilles reservation.
A strong wind gust lofted a 70 pound garbage can into the air at least 90 feet passing over pine trees 2 miles WSW of Aitkin.
Strong winds blew down numerous trees and ripped metal roofs off some structures in the Aitkin area. Local law enforcement said the damage continued east through the county towards the McGregor area.
Photos were received showing a building at the Aitkin County fairgrounds that had been blown over along with sheet metal that had been blown into the crown of a tree.
Multiple trees greater than 12 inches in diameter were downed along Hessman Hill Road.
A tree was downed onto a power line and then started on fire.
Eight trees were downed between the reporter's location and the home next door on Red Sand Lake. The trees fell during a 5 minute period at the onset of the storm.
Several trees were downed by the winds near the North Memorial Ambulance Station in downtown Brainerd.
A large tree was down on the road at the spotter's location.
A photo was received showing a tree that fell across a road nearly landing on a parked car.
A large tree was down across Blueberry Island road and needed to be removed by the county public works department.
A few 3 inch diameter tree limbs were broken.
A washout was reported along Breezy Lane in Finland.
Multiple washouts were reported along Cramer Road near and east of Finland.

A photo was received showing Moose Valley Road flooded at Carlson Creek with water flowing over the road surface. A later report indicated the Cook County Highway Department closed the road at 6:30 AM CDT.
A gust of 59 mph was recorded by the ASOS at the Brainerd Airport.
A gust of 61 mph was measured at the Brainerd Airport.
Water was over Cook County Road 60 and County State Aid Highway 14 with multiple culvert washouts. A No Travel Advisory was issued by the county for this area due to the water and damage.

Dozens of trees were found to be bent or uprooted in the area.

Around 50 trees were downed on the reporter's property on the east side of Grand Lake. Most trees were 12 to 16 inches in diameter with some completely uprooted. Some of the trees fell on power lines leading to power outages. The trees were all at least 30 years old. No structure damage was reported at the location.

A brief tornado tracked approximately west to east from north of the intersection of Lismore Road and Arnold Road, across Eagle Lake Road, and then across Jean Duluth Road before ending near Lady Nicole Lane east of Jean Duluth Road. This tornado caused numerous tree damage along its path, with a consistent tree fall pattern indicative of a tornado, but was unlikely above EF-0 in strength. While a few trees were snapped near the base, the vast majority of tree damage was large branches and trees that have bent over, with a few uprooted trees. The estimated maximum wind speed of this tornado was 85 mph. There was no known property damage outside of the tree damage.

Part of a roof was ripped off a house along with part of a wall attached to a screen porch blown down. Approximately 10 trees as large as a foot and a half to two feet in diameter were down along with a pine tree that was snapped.

A tornado caused damage in southwest Cass County, mainly across Poplar Township. The tornado began near the Poplar Cemetery and tracked north-northeast. Around a dozen power poles were snapped near the base along 60th St SW to the west of Highway 64 along with numerous tree damage, including several very healthy pine trees with trunks 12-18 inches in diameter snapped at the base. A small piece of farm equipment was also tossed roughly 100 yards. Significant tree damage was observed along Highway 64 around the intersection of 56 St SW, with damage continuing to the northeast into a wetland/bog-type landscape that was inaccessible. Peak winds were estimated to be 105 mph.

A brief tornado started near the intersection of County Road 63 and Becker road. The tornado tracked north-northeast, sporadically knocking down trees along the way. While the tree damage was not as significant as other storms on this day, drone imagery provided by a spotter depicted a very clearly convergent signature in the tree damage. The most significant damage from this tornado was the partial lifting off of a roof from a two story home, though no broken windows were noted and |otherwise shingle damage appeared very minor. Sporadic tree damage continued in a path to the north towards the Mississippi River where the damage path appeared to end. Peak winds were estimated to be 85 mph.

A tornado produced a path of damage through the city of Deer River, with damage to numerous homes and businesses. The tornado likely began somewhere just south of Highway 2, though a precise location was difficult to determine due to a lack of |damage. The first damage observed was a camper/RV that was in a parking lot south of Highway 2 which was tossed across the highway into the parking lot of a furniture store building just north of the highway. The furniture store building had all of its south |facing windows blown out with damage to the front facade and some evidence of roof lift on the flat portion of the roof. The building also lost part of a gabled metal roof. A metal shed/outbuilding in the parking lot was completely destroyed. To the north, a two story building that includes a funeral home and post office had evidence of roof lift. Continuing north through the residential streets numerous trees were downed and several outbuildings - sheds and garage buildings - sustained significant damage, with some collapsing and others sliding off their foundations. This damage continued north- northwest, crossing state highway 6 around 7th Ave. Damage to the ball fields north of|town are believed to be part of the tornado���s path, with a small outbuilding and dugouts being destroyed and damage sustained to the metal chain link fence. Tree damage continued onto private property to the northwest, with the end of the tornado path estimated to be near or just south of County Road 142. Peak winds were estimated to be 107 mph.

Damage sustained to a fast food restaurant in Hinckley, including broken windows, a damaged rooftop HVAC unit, and evidence of metal flashing damage, is believed to be the beginning of a tornado that then tracked across Interstate 35 in a north-northwest direction, crossing the railroad tracks near 7th St NE. The majority of the damage was trees uprooted with several snapped along the way. Aerial imagery provided by the Pine County Sheriff���s Department shows fairly weak but convergent tree fall between I-35 and near Highway 61 and Owl Drive between a distinct intensification where the treefall becomes much more extensive and a metal roof section was lifted off a local business. The tornado then tracked across Highway 61 and traversed north causing mainly tree damage with at least one home losing some roof shingles. The end of the tornado path is estimated due to the track moving into a much less wooded wetland area. NWS Duluth sincerely appreciates the drone imagery provided by the Pine County Sheriff���s Office to aid in the assessment of this storm damage. Peak winds were estimated to be 95 mph.

A spring storm coupled with frost leaving the ground led to excessive runoff that resulted in damage to two culverts. Pictures show culverts being pushed upward. Protection on the road was necessary due to sinkholes that opened up above the culverts. Both culverts will need replacing. Each culvert is 84 inches by 70 feet with preliminary estimated costs of $20,000 to replace culverts and make repairs to the road along with time and equipment. The Town of Baronett requested an emergency declaration to help cover the costs.

A local TV meteorologist forwarded photos from a viewer showing a culvert that had washed out on Hill Road near Floodwood. There was a roughly 6 foot gap in the road that was at least 3 to 4 feet deep where the flow of the creek exceeded the capacity of the culvert and washed out the road. The viewers that sent the photos were unable to leave their property by vehicle and had to make a makeshift footbridge to get to town.

Heavy rainfall led to the Poplar River becoming swollen and raging. Trees and other debris significantly damaged two covered bridges near the mouth of the river at the Lutsen Resort. The older of the two bridges was built in 1930 with the other dating from the 1950s. The resort owners have vowed to rebuild the bridges. Additionally, hundreds of trees were wiped out by the water as well.

A school bus became stranded in flood waters when the shoulder washed out underneath it and it partially tipped. Four students and the driver were helped from the bus to safety and there were no injuries reported, although the bus driver was taken to the hospital to be checked out. The bus went through the flooded section of road 15 minutes prior to returning and trying to make it through a second time.

At approximately 2:38PM CDT on the afternoon of the 7th, La Pointe Police, La Pointe Fire and Madeline Island EMS were dispatched to Big Bay State Park at the southeast corner of the island for a man that was cliff jumping at the Eagle's Nest cliffs and did not resurface. The man had completed one jump and on the second, succumbed to the rough surf conditions in place (41, M). He was alone in the water at the time. Winds were from the NNE at around 10 mph with gusts to around 20 mph at the time with waves around 2 to 4 feet. A Small Craft Advisory was in effect at the time. The man's body was not recovered until the early afternoon on the 8th. Multiple agencies assisted with the search and recovery efforts including the Wisconsin DNR, US Park Service, USCG, Bayfield Fire Dive Team, Sawyer County Dive Team, Sawyer County Search and Rescue, Ashland County Sheriffs Office, Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission and Mashkiiziibii Conservation Wardens from the Bad River Tribe. In a separate incident just east of Ashland on Chequamegon Bay, a 60 year old man was last seen fishing during the afternoon hours alone amid the large waves and windy conditions. His empty boat was found washed ashore the next morning (Monday) near Second Landing Water Access and he was reported missing when he failed to report for work that morning. His body was located about a half-mile from where his boat washed ashore Thursday night (60, M). While a Small Craft Advisory was in effect on Lake Superior, one was not in effect for the waters of Chequamegon Bay.

Two men were boating on Lake Superior off Iron County during the morning hours of Thursday the 25th. Northeast winds of 10 to 15 knots with gusts to 25 knots were reported during the early morning hours with waves of 3 to 5 feet. A Small Craft Advisory was in effect. Iron County Sheriff's Office received a 911 call around 8:55AM CDT that morning from one of the men in the boat reporting that the boat had capsized near Marble Point. Due to the water conditions and lack of road access to the Marble Point area, it took rescuers additional time to reach the two men. One of the men (64, M) had died and rescuers brought the other man to shore where he declined medical attention. The rescue process lasted until just after 4PM CDT.

Easterly winds gusting in excess of 50 mph off Lake Superior led to widespread reports of damage in the Duluth area and up the North Shore in southern St. Louis County. Numerous reports of trees down with some on power lines along with debris blocking roads were received. Additionally, damage to public infrastructure was reported as well. A State of Local Disaster was declared for St. Louis County as a result of the storm. A max gust for the event of 54 mph was recorded at the Duluth International Airport.

Easterly winds gusting in excess of 50 mph generated waves of 8 to 13 feet along the North Shore of Lake Superior in southern St. Louis County. These waves led to extensive damage and erosion along the shoreline. The worst damage was seen in the Brighton Park area of Duluth. Due to other events like this over the past 5 years, mitigation and restoration was still ongoing at the time of this event. The Brighton Beach area in Duluth in particular was hit hard with the loss of material being used in the restoration and mitigation work in addition to new damage as well.

Snowfall totals across the northern part of the county were in the 6 to 8 inch range for the event with a high report of 8.5 inches near Ely.

The highest totals across the northern portions of Lake and Cook counties was along the terrain ridge in the southern reaches of the area where some lake enhancement occurred. Totals tapered off to the north of the terrain ridge and were below 6 inches, but picked up again further north where 8.7 inches was recorded at the COOP site 25 miles east of Ely on Snowbank Lake.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were recorded across the northern part of Itasca County with a high report of 8 inches about 13 miles north of Bovey.

Snowfall totals along the terrain ridge of southern Lake County were higher than expected due to lake enhancement. Totals of 5 to 10 inches were reported along the terrain ridge with 2 to 4 inches near Lake Superior. The highest report came from just west of Silver Bay were 15 inches was reported while Silver Bay itself only received around 5 inches showing the tight gradient along the ridge.

Snowfall totals along the terrain ridge of southern Cook County were higher than expected due to lake enhancement. Totals of 6 to 12 inches were reported across this area with a high report of 15 inches near Hovland.

Snowfall totals around the southern portion of St. Louis County and Carlton County were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range. Some lake enhancement was observed on the northeast side of Duluth where around 8 inches was recorded.

A strong low pressure system brought heavy late season snow to the area on the 29th into the 30th. While much of the snow was lost to melting with higher sun angles and rain falling on the snow at times, parts of the county did report snowfall as high as around 8 inches in the Mellen area.

While much of the snow was lost to melting with higher sun angles and rain falling on the snow at times, parts of the county did report snowfall of 6 to 8 inches with the Gile area receiving around 10.5 inches by the time the system ended.

Warm temperatures early in April led to rapid snowmelt of a well above normal snowpack across the region. Additionally, heavy rainfall on top of the snowpack led to additional high runoff across the county as well. Roads began to be impacted on the 11th with water overtopping low spots leading to washouts and failed culverts. Temperatures cooled during the middle of the month along with a heavy snow event the 16th into the 17th. This allowed the runoff to slow and water levels to drop. All major roads were reported back open by the 18th. Multiple communities in addition to the county issued disaster declarations due to the extent of washed out roads. The Town of Superior estimated $100,000 in damages from the flooding, which was the highest report from an entity in the county.

High water continued to impact homes, driveways and farm fields into the latter portion of the month.

Two 18 year old males died while cliff jumping at Black Beach in Silver Bay. The two jumped from the cliff just before 1:30PM CDT on the 25th and were seen struggling in the water before slipping beneath the waves. Waves at the time were in the 3 to 6 foot range with northeast winds gusting to 20 to 25 knots. Additionally the lake temperatures were in the lower 40s Fahrenheit. The Lake County Sheriff's office cited the winds, waves and water temperatures as contributing the drownings. Small Craft Advisories were in effect highlighting the hazardous conditions in the area.

A small sliver of D2 Significant Drought was added to far southwestern Pine County with the update on the 13th and persisted through the remainder of the month. A small sliver of far northeastern Pine County was added to the D2 Severe Drought area with the update on the 20th. Rainfall deficits in excess of 2.5 inches were observed across much of Pine County which is about 50 to 70 percent of normal for the month of June.

Landspout. Location: 48.054697N / 92.831284W. Video was received from an Orr fire department member via a local TV meteorologist showing a landspout moving through Orr. Some small debris was seen lofted at times along with the rotation followed by trees swaying heavily in the wind as the center of circulation passed over. Another video from a boat on Pelican Lake looking east at Orr showing rotation in the clouds aloft along with a ground circulation. The landspout may have started as a waterspout over Pelican Lake, but this was not evident in the videos received, only by the radar depiction of the parent shower. No damage was reported and the time and location were estimated.
Rainfall at the end of June was enough to lift the far southwestern corner of southern Lake County out of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 4th. However, D1 Moderate Drought remained in place.

July began with D2 Severe Drought across the far southeastern reaches of St. Louis County and the far eastern reaches of Carlton County with D1 Moderate Drought prevailing elsewhere. Some rain at the end of June into early July led to a brief period of improvement with the updates on the 4th and the 11th which saw a reduction in the coverage of D2 Severe Drought. However, rainfall became quite sparse starting around the middle of the month with D2 Severe Drought spreading across all of Carlton County with the update on the 25th and back into southeastern and far southern St. Louis County as well. Rainfall deficits  of 2 to 3 inches below normal for the month were observed across the region.

July began with small areas of D2 Severe Drought across the far northeastern and southwestern corners of Pine County with D1 Moderate Drought elsewhere across the county. Dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw D2 Severe Drought expand across most of the remainder of the county by the end of the month aside of areas along the St. Croix River. Rainfall deficits of 1 to 3 inches were observed across the county with northern areas seeing the greatest departures from normal.

July began with D2 Severe Drought across the southern portion of the county with D1 Moderate Drought elsewhere across the county. Conditions worsened as the month progressed with the area seeing rainfall deficits of 3 to 4 inches plus. All of the county was under D2 Severe Drought by the update on the 25th and continued to worsen through the remainder of the month.

July began with a small area of D1 Severe Drought across the far southern reaches of southern Aitkin County with D0 Abnormally Dry elsewhere across the county. Dry conditions over the month saw D2 Severe Drought introduced with the update on the 11th and then expanding northward across the remainder of the southern part of the county by 25th. Rainfall deficits for the month of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the county.

July began with D0 Abnormally Dry conditions across the county with most of the county then being downgraded to D1 Moderate Drought conditions with the update on the 4th. Continued dry conditions over the month saw D2 Severe Drought introduced with the update on the 18th across the southwestern corner of the county and then persisting through the remainder of the month. Rainfall deficits for the month of 1 to 3 inches were observed across the county.

July began with D0 Abnormally Dry conditions across all of Itasca County with D1 Moderate Drought quickly entering the picture for most of the county with the update on the 4th. Continued dry conditions over the month saw the introduction of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 18th across the far western area of the county and then persisting through the remainder of the month. Rainfall deficits for the month of 1 to 2 inches were observed across the county.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions across much of northern Cass County with D2 Severe Drought entering the picture across far northern areas with the update on the 18th. Continued dry conditions over the month led to the area of D2 Severe Drought persisting through the remainder of the month. Rainfall deficits for the month of 1 to 3 inches were observed across the northern part of county.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions across southern Cass County. Continued dry conditions over the month led to D2 Severe Drought being introduced across the entire southern part of the county with the update on the 25th and persisting through the remainder of the month. Rainfall deficits for the month of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the southern part of county.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions across much of northern Aitkin County. Continued dry conditions over the month led to the introduction of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 25th across the southern half of the northern part of the county that persisted through the remainder of the month. Rainfall deficits for the month of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the northern part of county.

After improving to D1 Moderate Drought early in the month, continued dry conditions led to the reintroduction of D2 Severe Drought across the far southeastern corner of southern Lake County with the update on the 25th. These conditions then persisted through the remainder of the month with rainfall deficits of 1 to 2 inches for the month.

July began with D2 Severe Drought across the northwestern half of the county with D1 Moderate Drought for the southeast half. D2 Severe Drought slowly expanded across the remainder of the county by the 25th and D3 Extreme Drought was introduced on the 18th across much of the northern third of the county as rainfall deficits of 1 to 3 inches were observed for the month.

July began with D2 Severe Drought across the far northwestern corner of the county. D2 Severe Drought spread across the northern half of the county by the 11th and continued working south over the next two weeks before encompassing the southern part of the county as well by the 25th. D3 Extreme Drought was introduced on the 18th across the northwestern quarter of the county and along much of the Bayfield Peninsula. Much of the county was within an inch of normal precipitation for the month, but the sandy soil continued to dry leading to worsening drought conditions.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions covering the county. An area of D2 Severe Drought spread into the Ashland area and the Apostle Islands with the update on the 11th. D2 Severe Drought spread across the northern half of the county by the 18th and then much of the southern part of the county by the 25, with just the southeastern corner remaining in D1 Moderate Drought. Rainfall for the month was generally within a inch of normal, both above and below, but the sandy soil continued to dry as the month progressed.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions covering the county. An area of D2 Severe Drought spread into the southeastern corner of the county with the update on the 11th. D2 Severe Drought then spread across much of the remainder of the county by the 25th outside of a small sliver in the far southwestern corner. Rainfall for the month was around 2 to 4 inches below normal and was exacerbated by the sandy soil.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions covering the county. D2 Severe Drought spread across most of the county with the update on the 11th aside from the northeastern and eastern reaches of the county. The area of D2 Severe Drought expanded with the update on the 25th, leaving only the far eastern reaches of the county in D1 Moderate Drought. Rainfall for the month varied across the county with deficits of 1 to 3 inches over much of the county outside of the northeastern reaches where slightly above normal rainfall fell.

July began with D1 Moderate Drought conditions covering the county. An area of D2 Severe Drought spread into the southwestern quarter of the county on the 11th. D2 Severe Drought then retreated to the extreme southwestern corner with the update on the 18th with no further changes over the remainder of the month. This was despite most of the county seeing rainfall deficits of 1 to 2 inches outside of the northwestern corner which received slightly above normal rainfall for the month.

July began with D0 Abnormally Dry and D1 Moderate Drought conditions across the county. D1 Moderate Drought spread across the entire county with the update on the 11th before D2 Severe Drought was added across the northern portion of the county on the 18th. There was a very slight increase in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 25th as rainfall deficits of 1 to 3 inches for the month led to worsening conditions.

Drought conditions were slower to impact Burnett County with D1 Moderate Drought prevailing for most of the month outside of a small, brief area of D0 Abnormally Dry conditions during the middle of the month. Rainfall deficits of 1 to 3 inches for the month led to D2 Severe Drought being introduced with the update on the 25th across the far northern reaches of the county.

Two swimmers were rescued after being caught in a rip current along the Park Point beach near the Duluth Aerial Lift Bridge. The swimmers were two juvenile females that stated that they were swept out into the lake while swimming in waist to chest deep water. One of the swimmers said that she was wading in the waves and was instantly swept off of her feet. She began to be taken out into the lake. Her friend came into the water to save her and was also caught in the rip current. Upon arrival, Duluth Fire learned that the swimmers were rescued by a passerby. The rescuer was walking the beach with a companion and said that he heard the cry for help. He reported that one of the swimmers had mostly made it to shore. He quickly went for the second swimmer. Both of the swimmers were safely retrieved and examined by paramedics, but did not require medical care.

August began with a small area of D2 Severe Drought across the far southwestern corner of Koochiching County. This area expanded slightly with the update on the 22nd with no additional worsening of drought conditions over the remainder of the month. Most of the county only received around 50-70 percent of normal rainfall for the month, but areas around International Falls actually saw above normal rainfall for the month.

August began with just a small area of D2 Severe Drought across the far southwestern corner of southern Lake County. Rainfall for the month was around 50 to 70 percent of normal, but no change in the area of D2 Severe Drought was observed through the month.

August begin with D2 Severe Drought conditions across all of Carlton County and adjacent areas of southern St. Louis County and into the southeastern reaches of southern St. Louis as well. A small sliver if D3 Extreme Drought was added to extreme eastern Carlton County with the update on the 8th. Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across all of Carlton County and extreme southeastern southern St. Louis County with the update on the 29th. Rainfall for the month was only around 25 to 50 percent of normal which led to the worsening conditions at the end of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the far western portion of northern Itasca County. This area expanded a bit to the east with the update on the 22nd and encompassed roughly the western third of the northern part of the county. Very dry conditions were observed through the month with less than 25 percent of normal rainfall falling. Some areas in the central part of the county received less than 5 percent of normal rainfall for the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the far western portions of southern Itasca County. This area expanded a bit to the east with the update on the 22nd and encompassed roughly the western third of the southern part of the county. Very dry conditions were observed through the month with less than 25 percent of normal rainfall falling. Some areas in the central part of the county received less than 5 percent of normal rainfall for the month.

All of northern Cass County was placed into D2 Severe Drought on the first of the month before a pocket of D1 Moderate Drought was introduced in the Leech Lake area on the 8th. Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw the entire northern part of the county once again in D2 Severe Drought conditions by the 22nd with D3 Extreme Drought being added in far southern areas with the update on the 29th. Portions of the southern part of northern Cass County actually received above normal precipitation for the month while the remainder of the area received about 70 to 90 percent of normal rainfall.

All of southern Cass County was in D2 Severe Drought for the majority of the month. Continued dry conditions through the month saw the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought into the entirety of the area with the update on the 29th. Portions of the northeastern part of southern Cass County actually received above normal precipitation for the month while the remainder of the area received about 70 to 90 percent of normal rainfall.

Crow Wing County began the month in D2 Severe Drought but the central portion of the county was upgraded to D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the morning of the first. This area of D3 Extreme Drought was slowly reduced over the next two weeks and was completely gone by the 15th. The extreme southern portion of the county also improved to D1 Moderate Drought with this update as well. Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw D2 Severe Drought return over the entire county by the 22nd with D3 Extreme Drought returning to the northern three-quarters of the county by the 29th. Rainfall amounts around 70 percent of normal were observed across the southern part of the county with the northern part seeing slightly above normal rainfall for the month.

Southern Aitkin County began the month in D2 Severe Drought but the west-central portion of the county was upgraded to D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the morning of the first. This area of D3 Extreme Drought was removed with the update on the 15th. Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw D3 Extreme Drought returning to the northern two-thirds of the southern part of the county by the 29th. Rainfall amounts around 50 to 70 percent of normal were observed across the southern part of the county for the month.

Northern Aitkin County began the month with a mixture of D1 Moderate Drought across the northern half of the northern part of the county with D2 Severe Drought across the southern half. The area of D2 Severe Drought was expanded across the northwestern quarter of the northern half of the county with the update on the morning of the first.  Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw D2 Severe Drought expanding across the much of the remainder of the northern half of the county with the update on the 22nd with D3 Extreme Drought being introduced across the southern half of the northern part of the county on the 29th. Rainfall amounts around 50 to 70 percent of normal were observed across the northern part of the county for the month.

Pine County began the month with D2 Severe Drought across most of the county along with a small area of D1 Moderate Drought along the St. Croix River. The area of D2 Severe Drought was expanded across the remainder of the county with the update on the morning of the first.  Some improvement was noted with the update on the 15th as D1 Moderate Drought was added across the southwestern corner of the county. Continued dry conditions over the remainder of the month saw D2 Severe Drought expanding across the entire county once again with the update on the 22nd with D3 Extreme Drought being introduced across the northern quarter the county on the 29th. Rainfall amounts around 50 to 70 percent of normal were observed across the county for the month with the greatest deficits across the northern part of the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over most of the county with an area of D3 Extreme Drought across much of the northern part of the county. The area of D3 Extreme Drought spread across the remainder of the northern part of the county with the update on the 8th and an area of D4 Exceptional Drought was added in the far northeastern corner of the county as well. The area of D4 Exceptional Drought expanded a bit more to the west with the update on the 15th before a slight expansion of the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 29th. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over most of the county with an area of D3 Extreme Drought across the northwestern quarter of the county and along the shore of the Bayfield Peninsula. Some improvement was quickly seen on the morning of the first with D1 Moderate Drought spreading across the southern third of the county. The area of D3 Extreme Drought spread across the remainder of the northern part of the county with the update on the 8th and an area of D4 Exceptional Drought was added in the far northern areas of the county along Lake Superior as well. The area of D4 Exceptional Drought and D3 Extreme Drought expanded a bit more to the south with the update on the 15th along with D2 Severe Drought returning to far southern areas. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over most of the county with an area of D1  Moderate Drought across the southeastern corner of the county. Some improvement was quickly seen on the morning of the first with D1 Moderate Drought spreading across the southern two-thirds of the county. D2 Severe Drought then spread across the entire county with the update on the 15th along with a slight area of D3 Extreme Drought in the Ashland area. No additional changes were seen over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over the northern half of the county with D1  Moderate Drought across the southern half. Some improvement was quickly seen on the morning of the first with D1 Moderate Drought spreading across the southern two-thirds of the county. D2 Severe Drought then spread across most of the county with the update on the 15th. No additional changes were seen over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with a small area of D2 Severe Drought over the far southeastern corner of the county. D2 Severe Drought then spread into much of the far northern part of the county with the update on the 15th along with another small area spreading into the southeastern corner on the 22nd. Further expansion was seen on the 29th with D2 Severe Drought covering the western third of the county along with another area in the southeastern corner. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over most of the county. Some improvement was quickly seen on the morning of the first with D1 Moderate Drought spreading across far northern and far eastern areas, but an area of D3 Extreme Drought was also introduced in the far west-central portion of the county. D2 Severe Drought then spread across much of the remainder of the county with the update on the 15th. A slight expansion of the area of D3 Extreme Drought was introduced on the 22nd with D2 Severe Drought filling in the remaining areas on the 29th. Rainfall for the month was around 50 to 70 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought over most of the county. An area of D3 Extreme Drought was introduced in the central portion of the county with the update on the morning of the first. This area of D3 Extreme Drought expanded to encompass much of the county with the update on the 22nd aside from areas in the far corners of the county. No additional changes were observed over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was around 70 percent of normal across the county.

The month began with D1 Moderate Drought over most of the county with a small area of D2 Severe Drought across the far northeastern corner. D2 Severe Drought expanded into areas along the St. Croix River and the far eastern reaches of the county with the update on the morning of the first before spreading across the entire county on the 8th. Some minor improvement was seen on the 15th in the southwestern corner as D1 Moderate Drought spread in. This improvement was short-lived as D2 Severe Drought spread back across the entire county on the 22nd. No additional changes were observed over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was around 50 percent of normal across the county.

Photos were received from a spotter on the south end of Benoit Lake showing tree damage to their property. They reported 10 large trees down on their property with one landing on their garage causing minor damage. The spotter also estimated that there were hundreds of trees down in the area between Benoit and Rice lakes. Pea to dim sized hail also fell and was covering the ground in the photos as well.
Photos were received of large tree limbs at least two feet in diameter down in Hoyt Lakes.

Numerous trees were down onto power lines just off County Road 7 near Old Mesaba and Ramshaw roads and the CN Railroad tracks. Tree limbs ranged in diameter from 4 to 12 inches and were broken about 20 feet off the ground. The trees were a mix of popples, pines and maples.
Numerous trees were reported down on Boga Lake in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.
Photos were received showing several small to medium sized trees that were down along with power lines down as well.
Multiple large trees were down and the power was out.
Strong winds with the storms knocked down several trees along Vermilion Trail.
Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped off along Bass Lake Road. One of the trees fell onto an RV causing extensive damage to the RV.
Photos were received of several trees that were snapped off.
The storm blew the top off of a white pine tree and the spotters location.
Photos were received showing four pine tree trunks that had been snapped about halfway up. The trees were estimated to be about one foot in diameter.
A photo was received showing a large tree snapped and multiple other trees down around a campsite.
Vinyl siding was peeled off of a garage by the storm.
Multiple 12 to 18 inch pine trees were snapped at the location. The diameter was estimated from photos taken during the survey.

Numerous 12 inch plus diameter pine trees were snapped or uprooted at the location with one of the trees falling on an outbuilding. The tree diameter was estimated from photos taken during the survey.
A large evergreen tree was uprooted and fell onto a garage. The estimated diameter of the tree was 14 to 18 inches based on photos taken on the scene.
Multiple eight to 12 inch diameter pine trees were uprooted with the diameter of the trees estimated by photos taken on site.
Multiple eight to ten inch pine and aspen trees were snapped or uprooted with the diameter estimated by photos taken during the survey.
Many large trees were snapped off ten feet above the ground with trees nearby uprooted in areas with thin or wet soils. One tree limb was through the metal roof of a cabin.
Several large trees were snapped and a 24 inch diameter tree was uprooted.
