Thunderstorms over parts of Duluth dropped upwards of 3 to 6 inches of rain over a localized area focused on the Chester Creek basin over a period of 2 to 3 hours. The highest rainfall totals were located at the top of the hill in the College of St. Scholastica area. Flash flooding was reported upstream from this location along Arrowhead Road where 3 to 6 inches of water was flowing over the road where Chester Creek passed under the road. As the surge of water flowed downstream, it damaged walkways along the creek and sent 2 to 5 inches of water onto side streets and Kenwood Avenue. Chester Creek runs through tunnels for much of its trip down the Duluth hillside and this volume of water overwhelmed the tunnels sending a large stream of rapidly flowing water 3 to 10 inches deep down the hill. This affected a few apartment buildings in the vicinity of 7th Avenue and 3rd Street which required a few rescues/evacuations of lower level residents and pets in the buildings by the fire department. Interstate 35 runs through tunnels underground at the base of the hill and the water surging down the hillside began to collect in the tunnels. Standing and flowing water in the tunnels resulted in the closure of the tunnels for a period. Water of at least 4 to 6 inches in depth was covering the southbound lanes in spots. The water receded during the early morning hours of the 12th with cleanup occurring over the remainder of the week.

Heavy rainfall from backbuilding thunderstorms over Duluth led to 2 to 5 inches of rainfall in 2-3 hours. As the water rushed down the hillside to Lake Superior, it scoured out gravel alleys and sent around 1,000 cubic yards of construction debris, including sand, dirt, rock and other materials, onto Superior Street at the base of the hill. Superior Street at First Avenue East was closed for much of the 12th as crews worked to remove the piles of debris using heavy machinery.

Rainfall amounts of 5 to 7 inches were recorded across the Schmidt Creek basin on the 23rd and 24th with the vast majority of the rainfall occurring on the 24th. This amount of water was significantly more than the creek could handle and issues began near the headwaters. A small culvert carrying the creek under Pioneer Junction Road failed starting with a sinkhole in the road before the fast moving waters completely scoured a channel through the road. Further downstream just after passing under Minnesota Highway 61, the rapidly flowing water encountered another too small culvert that carried the creek under the tracks of the North Shore Scenic Railroad. The water proceeded to scour out this culvert as well exposing a bridge that was originally built by the railroad at this location over 100 years prior. An NSSR train had passed over the bridge about an hour before the culvert failed and noted the developing washout. The train was then stranded in Two Harbors until the washout could be repaired a few days later.
Rapidly flowing water was observed along Pitt Street in the Lakeside neighborhood of Duluth.

Rainfall amounts of 4 to 6 inches were observed on the 23rd and 24th with the vast majority falling during the morning of the 24th. Tischer Creek was overwhelmed by the water across much of its run through Duluth. Water was backed up across a large portion of the Ridgeview Country Club damaging bridges along the course. Water was also flowing through neighborhoods across streets and open areas with water over a foot deep in places. The main affects were observed across the Woodland and Hunter's Park neighborhoods of Duluth.

Amity Creek was out of its banks following 3 to 5 inches of rainfall. The surging water damaged a gazebo along the creek along with numerous pedestrian bridges covering them with logs and other detritus.
Fast flowing water 3 to 6 inches deep was running across yards and West Palm Street just upstream from the beginning of Coffee Creek in the Duluth Heights neighborhood.

Rainfall amounts of 5 to 7 inches were reported across much of Lakewood Township on the 24th leading to widespread flooding and flash flooding across the area. The Lester River was also out of its banks in the area. The flowing water washed out a few culverts and roads along Superior Street between Lakewood and McQuade roads. One spotter sent in photos of a river running through their normally dry yard that was 3 to 6 inches deep and moving quickly.

The heavy rainfall led to Miller Creek spilling out of its banks and flooding parking lots in the vicinity of Maple Grove Road and Mall Drive in the Miller Hill Mall area. The water was around 6 inches deep or deeper and was completely surrounding buildings in the area. Portions of Mall Drive between Maple Grove and Haines roads were also under water from Miller Creek as well. Due to poor drainage, the flooding lasted into the evening hours before receding.

D2 Severe Drought conditions were in place across far southwestern Koochiching County to begin the month. Rainfall for the month was roughly near normal across the county with far northwestern areas trending a bit below normal as much of the remainder of the county saw slightly above normal rainfall. Most if this rainfall fell over the latter half of the month. There was a slight expansion of the area of D2 Severe Drought across the southwestern quarter of the county with the update on the 5th followed by a reduction to just the far southwest corner with the update on the 26th. The remainder of the county remained in D1 Moderate Drought throughout the month.

The northern portion of Itasca County was a mix of D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought to begin the month. Roughly the western half of northern Itasca County was in D2 Severe Drought. Rainfall for the month was around a inch below normal across most of the area with the far northwestern corner seeing slightly above normal rainfall. With lingering dry conditions from August, D2 Severe Drought expanded across all of northern Itasca County with the update on the 5th. A very small area of D3 Extreme Drought was added at this time along the Mississippi River as well. Rainfall during the middle of the month led to a drastic reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 26th leaving only the far western quarter of the area in D2 Severe Drought. A very small area of D3 Extreme Drought remained in the far southwest corner of northern Itasca County adjacent to Lake Winnibigoshish. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The southern portion of Itasca County was a mix of D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought to begin the month. Roughly the western half of southern Itasca County was in D2 Severe Drought. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 3 inches above normal across most of the area with the central part of the area seeing slightly below normal rainfall. With lingering dry conditions from August, D2 Severe Drought expanded across all of southern Itasca County with the update on the 5th. An area of D3 Extreme Drought was added at this time along and south of the Mississippi River as well. Rainfall during the middle of the month led to a drastic reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 26th leaving only the areas along and south of the Mississippi in D2 Severe Drought along with the complete removal of the area of D3 Extreme Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The northern portion of Cass County was mainly covered by D2 Severe Drought with far southern areas in D3 Extreme Drought to begin the month. Rainfall for the month was around a inch below normal for areas north of Leech Lake while it was around an inch over normal over southern areas. With lingering dry conditions from August, D3 Extreme Drought expanded across all of northern Cass County with the update on the 5th. Rainfall during the middle of the month led to a reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 26th leaving the northwestern three-quarters of the area in D3 Extreme Drought with D2 Severe Drought elsewhere. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The southern portion of Cass County was mainly covered by D3 Moderate Drought to begin the month. Rainfall for the month was around a inch below normal for areas near the Crow Wing River while it was around an inch over normal over much of the remainder of the southern part of the county. Rainfall during the middle of the month led to a reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 26th leaving all of the area in D2 Severe Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

Cass County was mainly covered by D3 Moderate Drought to begin the month with a small area of D2 Severe Drought across the far southern reaches of the county. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 2 inches above normal across the county. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought to the entirety of the county by the update on the 12th. Rainfall during the middle of the month led to the removal of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 26th leaving all of the area in D2 Severe Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The northern portion of Aitkin County saw a mix of D3 Moderate Drought and D2 Severe Drought to begin the month. D2 Severe Drought covered the northern half of northern Aitkin County with D3 Extreme Drought across the southern half. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across the remainder of northern Aitkin County along with the introduction of a small area of D4 Exceptional Drought in the far southeastern corner of northern Aitkin County with the update on the 5th. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 3 inches above normal with much of it occurring over the latter half of the month. This led to a reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 19th in northeastern areas followed by a complete removal of D4 Exceptional Drought and D3 Extreme Drought across the area. While most of the area remained in D2 Severe Drought, a small area of D1 Moderate Drought was introduced in the northeastern corner of the county. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The southern portion of Aitkin County saw a mix of D3 Moderate Drought and D2 Severe Drought to begin the month. D2 Severe Drought covered the far southern reaches of the southern part of the county with D3 Extreme Drought across the remainder. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across the remainder of southern Aitkin County along with the introduction of a small area of D4 Exceptional Drought in the far northeastern corner of southern Aitkin County with the update on the 5th. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 3 inches above normal with much of it occurring over the latter half of the month. This led to the complete removal of D4 Exceptional Drought and D3 Extreme Drought across the area with the update on the 26th, leaving the area in D2 Severe Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across all of Carlton County and extreme southeastern St. Louis County with D2 severe drought over far southern St. Louis County. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought far southern St. Louis County as D2 Severe Drought expanded into the remainder of southern St. Louis County. Additionally, an area of D4 Exceptional Drought was added across the southwestern half of Carlton County. Rainfall for the month was around 3 to 6 inches plus above normal with much of it occurring over the latter half of the month, primarily during two heavy rainfall events that led to flash flooding in the Duluth area and along parts of the North Shore. This led to a reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought followed by the complete removal of D3 Extreme Drought and D4 Exceptional Drought  by the update on the 26th. While much of Carlton County and far southwestern southern St. Louis County remained in D2 Severe Drought, the remainder of the area improved to D1 Moderate Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

Pine County began the month with a mix of D3 Moderate Drought and D2 Severe Drought across the area. D2 Severe Drought covered the southern third of the county with D3 Extreme Drought across the northern third. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across the northern half of the county along with the introduction of a small area of D4 Exceptional Drought in the far northwestern corner of the county with the update on the 5th. Rainfall for the month was around 2 to 4 inches above normal with much of it occurring over the latter half of the month. This led to the complete removal of D4 Exceptional Drought and D3 Extreme Drought across the area with the update on the 26th, leaving the northern part of the county in D2 Severe Drought. No additional changes were noted over the last few days of the month.

September began with a small area of D2 Severe Drought across the southwestern corner of southern Lake County. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D2 Severe Drought across all of southern Lake County with the update on the 5th. A heavy rainfall event on September 11th led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought from southern Lake County with the update on the 12th. Another heavy rainfall event occurred later in the month resulting in rainfall of 4 to 7 inches above normal for the month. This helped improve the area to D0 Abnormally Dry by the end of the month.

September began with a mix of D1 Moderate Drought and D0 Abnormally Dry across the area. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D2 Severe Drought across the southern half of Lake County with the update on the 5th. A heavy rainfall event on September 11th led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought from southern Lake County with the update on the 12th. Rainfall of 1 to 3 inches above normal for the month helped improve most of the area to D0 Abnormally Dry by the end of the month.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across the northern half of the county with D2 Severe Drought across the southern half. Additionally, there was an area of D4 Exceptional Drought across the northeastern corner of the county. Lingering dry conditions from the end of August led to the expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across the southern half of the county with the update on the 5th. Multiple rainfall events followed for the second half of the month leading to improving conditions. The area of D4 Exceptional Drought was removed with the update on the 12th along with a reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought from the Superior area southeastward. Additional improvement was seen with the update on the 26th as all D3 Extreme Drought was removed leaving D2 Severe Drought for the southwestern quarter of the county and D1 Moderate Drought or D0 Abnormally Dry across the remainder of the county. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 4 inches above normal with even higher amounts adjacent to Lake Superior.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across the northern half of the county and D2 Severe Drought across the southern half. Additionally, there was an area of D4 Exceptional Drought across the northwestern corner of the county. Lingering dry conditions from the end of August led to the slight expansion of D3 Extreme Drought across far western areas of the county with the update on the 5th. Multiple rainfall events followed for the second half of the month leading to improving conditions. The area of D4 Exceptional Drought was removed with the update on the 12th and was replaced with D3 Extreme Drought while the remainder of the county improved to D2 Severe Drought. Additional improvement was seen with the update on the 26th as all D3 Extreme Drought was removed leaving D2 Severe Drought across most of the county and D1 Moderate Drought across the northwestern corner. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 4 inches above normal.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought in the Ashland area and D2 Severe Drought across the remainder of the county. Multiple rainfall events followed for the second half of the month leading to improving conditions. The area of D3 Extreme Drought was removed with the update on the 12th leaving D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the county with no additional changes over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was around 1 inch above normal.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across most of the county aside from a small area of D1 Moderate Drought in the far southeastern corner. D2 Severe Drought then spread across the entirety of the county with the update on the 5th.0 No additional changes were observed over the remainder of the month with rainfall for the month around 1 inch above normal.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the western half of the county and the southeastern corner with D1 Moderate Drought across the remainder of the county. Lingering dry conditions from August led to the expansion of D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the county with the update on the 5th. Below normal rainfall for the month by around 1 inch led to the introduction of D3 Extreme Drought across the southern two-thirds of the county with the update on the 19th. Some improvement was noted with the update on the 26th as the area of D3 Extreme Drought was reduced to the east-central portion of the county with D2 Severe Drought across the remainder of the county.

September began with D2 Severe Drought conditions across most of the county along with a small area of D3 Extreme Drought in the far west-central part of the county. The area of D3 Extreme Drought expanded slightly along the western border of the county with the update on the 5th, but was generally unchanged until the update on the 26th which saw the removal of D3 Extreme Drought from the county. A tiny area of D1 Moderate Drought was also added along the southern border with this update as well. Rainfall for the month was slightly above normal.

September began with D3 Extreme Drought conditions across most of the county along with D2 Severe Drought in the corners of the county. The area of D3 Extreme Drought expanded across most of the county with the update on the 5th, aside from a sliver of D2 Severe Drought in the far southwest corner. Slight improvement was seen with the update on the 12th as D2 Severe Drought was added in the northeastern corner of the county. All D3 Extreme Drought was removed from the county with the update on the 26th, leaving D2 Severe Drought across the county. Rainfall for the month was slightly above normal.

September began with D2 Severe Drought across all of the county. Lingering dryness from August saw the introduction of D3 Extreme Drought into the northeastern portion of the county. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 3 inches above normal which led to the removal of all D3 Extreme Drought from the county with the update on the 26th, leaving D2 Severe Drought across the northeastern third of the county with D1 Moderate Drought elsewhere.
Snowfall reports of 3 to 6 inches were received with a high report of 6.5 inches about 20 miles north of Two Harbors.
Snowfall of 4 to 8 inches was reported along the higher elevations of southern Lake County with a high report of 8.4 inches 7 miles north-northwest of Two Harbors.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 7 inches were reported across the central and northeastern part of the county with a high report of 7.4 inches near Solon Springs.
Snowfall totals of 3 to 6 inches were reported across the northwestern corner of the county with a high report of 7 inches near Iron River.

D2 Severe Drought conditions persisted through the month across the southwestern corner of the county. Some improvement was seen from D1 Moderate Drought to D0 Abnormally Dry across the eastern part of the county, however. Rainfall for the month was around 1 to 2 inches above normal across the central portion of the county.

D2 Severe Drought conditions were in place across the western quarter of northern Itasca County throughout the month with no changes observed. There was some improvement from D1 Moderate Drought to D0 Abnormally Dry across the eastern part of the county, however. Overall, rainfall for the month was within an inch of normal.

D2 Severe Drought conditions were in place across the far western reaches of southern Itasca County throughout the month with no changes observed. Overall, rainfall for the month was within an inch of normal.

October began with D3 Extreme Drought conditions over much of northern Cass County with D2 Severe Drought elsewhere. The area of D3 Extreme Drought was removed with the update on the 10th, but no additional chances were seen over the remainder of the month. Rainfall was near to slightly below normal over the course of the month.

The entirety of southern Cass County was covered with D2 Severe Drought throughout the month of October with no changes in status observed over the course of the month. Rainfall for the month was slightly below normal overall.

The entirety of Crow Wing County was covered with D2 Severe Drought to begin the month with a flight reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought in the east-central portion of the county near Lake Mille Lacs with the update on the 3rd. It was replaced with D1 Moderate Drought and no additional changes were seen over the remainder of the month. Rainfall for the month was slightly below normal overall.

October began with D2 Severe Drought over much of northern Aitkin County with a small area of D1 Moderate Drought over the northeastern corner. Further reductions in D2 Severe Drought were seen with the update on the 10th leaving roughly the eastern half of the county in D1 Moderate Drought and the western half in D2 Severe Drought. No additional changed were seen over the remainder of the month with rainfall for the month near to slightly below normal.

October began with D2 Severe Drought conditions across the entirety of southern Aitkin County. Most of the D2 Severe Drought conditions were removed with the updates on the 3rd and the 10th, leaving only areas near the Mississippi River in D2 Severe Drought. The remainder of the area was under D1 Moderate Drought conditions. No additional changes were seen over the remainder of the month with rainfall near to slightly below normal.

October began with D2 Severe Drought conditions across most of Carlton County outside of the far northeastern corner where D1 Moderate Drought was in place. Just the far southwestern corner of southern St. Louis County was in D2 Severe Drought as well. With the update on the 3rd, the southwestern corner of Carlton County was removed from D2 Severe Drought before all of southern St. Louis and Carlton counties were removed from D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 10th, leaving conditions ranging from none to D1 Moderate Drought. No additional changes of D2 Severe Drought or worse were then seen over the remainder of the month with rainfall around 1 to 2 inches below normal.

October began with D2 Severe Drought conditions across northern Pine County with D1 Moderate Drought across southern Pine County. With the update on the 3rd, most of northern Pine County was removed from D2 Severe Drought before all of county was removed from D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 10th, leaving conditions ranging from D0 Abnormally Dry to D1 Moderate Drought. No additional changes of D2 Severe Drought or worse were then seen over the remainder of the month with rainfall within an inch of normal.

October began with D2 Severe Drought across the southwestern quarter of the county with D1 Moderate Drought over the remainder outside of an area of D0 Abnormally Dry over the Superior area. Rainfall for the month was near to slightly below normal, but rainfall late in September and the early part of the month was enough to lead to the removal of D2 Severe Drought across the county with the update on the 10th. This left a mix of D0 Abnormally Dry across the northern part of the county with D1 Moderate Drought across the remainder of the county.

October began with D2 Severe Drought across most of the county with D1 Moderate Drought across the far northern part of the county adjacent to Lake Superior. Rainfall for the month was near to slightly below normal, but rainfall late in September and the early part of the month was enough to lead to the reduction of D2 Severe Drought to just the southwestern portion of the county with the update on the 10th. This left a mix of D1 Moderate Drought across much of the remainder of the county with D0 Abnormally Dry conditions across the far northern part of the county adjacent to Lake Superior. No additional changes were seen over the remainder of the month.

Freezing drizzle caused slick and hazardous road conditions during the early morning hours of the 30th. A driver lost control on the ice covered road near Hibbing just after 6AM. The vehicle fishtailed, crossed the center line and collided with an oncoming vehicle before leaving the road and rolling with the driver being ejected from the vehicle. The driver was not wearing a seatbelt and was transported to a regional hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries. The other driver was treated on scene and released. This was the most serious incident reported that morning among numerous reports of spinouts, wrecks and vehicles in ditches.

A large spring storm brought heavy snowfall to much of northeastern Minnesota the 24th into the 26th. Dry air at the surface let to a delayed start across Koochiching County, but snow ended up being a bit heavier than expected when temperatures remained cooler and mixed precipitation did not really occur. Snowfall totals of 7 to 11 inches were reported across the county with a high report of 11.7 inches in International Falls.

Tornado developed over Upper Whitefish Lake (no tornadic damage found or reported on the northwestern shore indicating the tornado touched down on land before crossing the lake) and traveled southeast towards Pelican Lake. Extensive damage to private residences and forest along Old Whiskey Road and Ruttger Rd (referred to by locals as ���Tip Top Point���) and across Bertha and Clamshell Lake towards the far eastern reach of Whitefish Golf Club���s holes. Damage path was the widest near Old Whiskey and Ruttger Road, around 700 yards across, with tree damage even identified on the island to the north of Old Whiskey Road. Over 80% of trees were uprooted or snapped near the base, and numerous homes showed minor to major roof damage. The worst of the roof damage was several homes which had over 50% of the roof deck uplifted and removed. Homeowners also reported a nearly hour-long storm surge of 1 to 2 feet from Upper Whitefish Lake. Minnesota State Patrol helicopter footage shows some scattered tornadic tree damage south of County Road 16 near Clear Lake before no additional damage has been found or reported. No fatalities or injuries reported.

A tornado redeveloped near Wolford, from the same storm that produced the first tornado near Crosslake. Initial damage located along County Road 30, south of County Highway 11/Mississippi River, mostly trees snapped and uprooted. Tornado continued east- southeast across Rabbit Lake just north of Cuyuna and then towards Highway 210. Damage along the western shore of Rabbit Lake affected private residences with a RV flipped over, roof covering material partially removed, and numerous trees snapped which lead to secondary home damage, including several collapsed out- buildings and garages. The tornado crossed Highway 210 near mile marker 145, as evidenced by both tree damage and storm chaser footage. It then took a southeastward path across portions of western Cedar Lake, producing extensive tree damage and pockets of residential property damage to roofs and garages, including a fish house that was picked up and thrown nearly 100 yards. This is the area of low-end EF-2 damage. The tornado path then continued southeast, crossing into Aitkin County before dissipating at 1904 CDT. The tornado was only rated EF-0 once crossing into Aitkin County. No fatalities or injuries were reported.

Another tornado developed on the northern portion of Hammal lake, where localized pockets of extensive tree damage were located, and one three-season cabin and boat house were completely destroyed and partially thrown into the water. The tornado continued east- southeast, uprooting and snapping several mature tree trunks as it crossed Highway 169 and Hanging Kettle Lake. The tornado then took a east-southeastward path through Ripple Lake, uprooting trees and knocking over an 85 foot tall antenna tower before the tornado ended over southeastern Ripple Lake. No fatalities or injuries were reported.

A third tornado developed near Glen, MN. Storm chaser and spotter video depict a wispy tornado with no debris visible. Due to the rural and forested nature of this damage and no reports of damage, a ground survey has not been completed. This tornado rating and details may be updated in the future as additional aerial imagery becomes available.

Tornado developed on or near the Aitkin/Carlton County line and traveled southeast towards Highway 210 between Wright and Cromwell. Minor tree damage was noted on West Road near the start of the tornado path, with a broad area of large branches down and a few trees snapped towards the top. The tornado then traveled across a mainly marsh/bog landscape, crossing Center Road where power lines were damaged and widespread tree damage was noted along a 50 yard stretch of road. The tornado track continued on a southeast to east-southeast path, with the last signs of damage near to just south of Highway 210 near Woodbury Lake where a few clusters of tree damage were noted. No injuries or fatalities were reported, and property damage was very limited, with only a handful of homes/buildings impacted.

Tornado damage initially appeared on the northeast shore of Tanner Lake (east of Dumbbell Lake), crossing Wanless Road (Forest Road 172) on a southeastward track. Satellite imagery depicts sporadic tree damage along the path, with a particularly impressive swath of trees that were uprooted or snapped east of East General Grade Road (Forest Road 362) measuring approximately 150 yards in width and a quarter mile in length. Damage continues to be evident for another mile or so before no additional discernible damage is evident. No fatalities or injuries were reported. Tornado rating was determined based on satellite imagery, and NWS Duluth is coordinating to learn more about any air or ground surveyed damage from our partners at the Superior National Forest which may result in a future revision in the tornado rating.

The tornado initially formed near Wolford in Crow Wing County and entered Aitkin County near the end of Cedar Lake Drive on Cedar Lake. The tornado path was to the southeast, crossing 456th Place, 320th Street, and, finally, 310th Street before lifting. This last section of the tornado path after Cedar Lake shows damage to numerous trees via satellite imagery before the visible damage path ends just to the southwest of the intersection of 310th Street and Pioneer Avenue. The tornado was rates as an EF-0 in Aitkin County, but produced EF-2 damage in Crow Wing County just before crossing into Aitkin County. No fatalities or injuries were reported.

A supercell thunderstorm formed halfway between Meadowlands and Canyon, MN, between 4:35 to 4:40 PM on Thursday, September 19, 2024. As the strong thunderstorm continued to show potential for producing a tornado, the National Weather Service office in Duluth, MN, issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning at 4:44 PM for this storm. The strong storm moved eastward over unpopulated marshes immediately north of Lake Nichols Road about 4 miles north-northwest of Canyon, MN, by 5:00 PM. Meteorologists at the National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for this storm at 4:55 PM as early signs of tornadic development appeared on radar, and a short time later a tornado was confirmed by trained spotters and law enforcement. Visible tree damage from the tornado, estimated to have begun at 5:05 PM CDT, was first observed on the west side of US Highway 53 about 4.5 miles south of Cotton, MN, with pine trees snapped at the base. The tornado continued to move northeastward to uproot trees along Three Lakes Road about one-half mile east of the U.S. Highway 53 intersection. The storm began to move more north-northeastward so the tornado track shifted more northward with the most widespread surveyed damage seen along Bug Creek Road about 2.5 miles east-southeast of Cotton, MN. Over 50 pine trees and numerous clusters of aspen trees were observed to be snapped at the base and/or uprooted, estimated to have occurred at around 5:15 PM. A few still-standing pine trees had metal sheets lofted and wrapped around them. Minor to moderate structure damage was reported by two property owners along Bug Creek Road before the tornado passed northward over the Whiteface River. Towards 5:18 PM, the tornado began to weaken and finally lifted off the ground. The last uprooted trees, 4 aspen, were last observed at the intersection of Comstock Lake Road and Melrude Road, 2.7 miles east of Cotton, MN. In total, the tornado was on the ground for a total of 5.9 miles and for around 13 minutes. The damage rating from the NWS Duluth Storm Survey team resulted in an EF-1 rating with winds estimated at 105 mph. There were a total of two Tornado Warning in effect from 4:55 PM to 5:45 PM for this tornadic supercell thunderstorm.

Continued precipitation during the early part of the month led to the complete removal of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 19th, leaving a mix of D1 Moderate Drought and D0 Abnormally Dry across the county. Overall precipitation for the month was around 1 to 2 inches above normal across the county.

Precipitation during the beginning and middle of the month led to the reduction of D2 Severe Drought across the southern half of northern Lake County and a small portion of the southwestern corner of northern Cook County with the update on the 19th. Complete removal of D2 Severe Drought conditions across was realized with the update on the 26th, leaving D0 Abnormally Dry conditions in place. Overall precipitation for the month was up to 2 inches above normal across most of the area with slightly below normal precipitation along the International Border.

Northwest winds gusting in excess of 50 mph during the early morning hours of the 11th led to widespread tree and power line damage across southern Cook County. Some of the downed power lines were reported to be sparking and smoking. During the height of the wind storm, the local power cooperative reported that 62 percent of its customers in the area were without power. Local public utility and highway departments spent the morning removing numerous trees across the area that had fallen onto roadways. The ASOS station at the Bay of Grand Marais reported a maximum wind gust of 55 mph just before 8AM during the event.

The bolt caused extensive damage to one of the homes on the cul-de-sac including blowing out two well systems, burning the electric lines into the home, damaged a water line along with a water heater and water softener, blew off multiple tongue and groove boards, insulation and soffit on the house and a shed, destroyed internet and phone lines and all equipment connected to it, and had several wires burn and melt, leading to a smoky haze in the home. The Jenkins Creek Fire ignited on Monday, May 12, 2025, around 1PM local time. It was detected east of County Road 110 and north of County Road 16 near Jenkins Creek, approximately 15 miles southeast of Hoyt Lakes, Minnesota. It was believed to have been started by a discarded cigarette from a passing vehicle. The fire rapidly expanded due to hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and strong south winds, burning through mixed boreal forest and grassy ground cover, including areas heavily infested by spruce budworm, which contributed to the fire's intensity.||The fire initially exhibited extreme behavior, including crown fires and rapid spread through dense forested areas. The presence of dead and dying trees, particularly those affected by spruce budworm infestations, provided ample fuel for the fire's growth. After a couple days, the spread slowed as crews responded, winds subsided, and moisture moved into the area. Firefighters were able to take advantage of that opportunity and built a line that held through another wind event a few days later. Since then, containment continued to be effectively established with full containment achieved on June 21st. The fire reached a maximum size of 16,490 acres.

The Camp House fire began on Sunday, May 11, 2025, at approximately 2PM local time in Ault Township, about two miles northeast of Brimson, Minnesota, outside the Superior National Forest. The fire was initially reported at 750 acres and expanded rapidly due to dry conditions, gusty winds, and a large volume of dead timber, particularly in areas infested with spruce budworms. It is believed to have been started by an unattended campfire. The fire moved into the Superior National Forest, causing closures and evacuations. Initial fire behavior included crown fires and rapid spread through dense forest, fueled by widespread dead and dying trees.||At least 144 structures, primarily homes and cabins along Highway 44, were destroyed by the fire's initial spread. Initially, mandatory evacuations were put in place for Highway 44 and nearby communities, and evacuation centers were established to assist displaced residents. ||On Wednesday, May 28, 2025, the the local Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) area forestry assumed management of the Camp House fire. Firefighting operations continued into June with the fire not being 100% contained until the morning of June 13th. The fire reached a maximum size of 12,071 acres and affected around 150 structures.

The Munger Shaw wildfire, located approximately ten miles southeast of Cotton, Minnesota, was detected late in the afternoon on Monday, May 12. Minnesota DNR, along with local fire departments, responded. Multiple aircraft were brought in to help slow down the active flame fronts, supporting the ground firefighting efforts. The fire was active in pine and lowland fuels, but favorable weather conditions led to slow growth of the fire. The fire was believed to have started with the spontaneous combustion of a hay bale. The fire was 95% contained by Monday, May 19th, but was not fully contained until June 13th. At one point during the early days of the fire, the mainline of the Canadian National Railroad was shut down as the fire spread to both sides of the tracks. The maximum size of the fire was 1,259 acres.

It was detected east of County Road 110 and north of County Road 16 near Jenkins Creek, approximately 15 miles southeast of Hoyt Lakes, Minnesota. It was believed to have been started by a discarded cigarette from a passing vehicle. The fire rapidly expanded due to hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and strong south winds, burning through mixed boreal forest and grassy ground cover, including areas heavily infested by spruce budworm, which contributed to the fire's intensity. The fire initially exhibited extreme behavior, including crown fires and rapid spread through dense forested areas. The presence of dead and dying trees, particularly those affected by spruce budworm infestations, provided ample fuel for the fire's growth. After a couple days, the spread slowed as crews responded, winds subsided, and moisture moved into the area. The Camp House fire began on Sunday, May 11, 2025, at approximately 2PM local time in Ault Township, about two miles northeast of Brimson, Minnesota, outside the Superior National Forest. The fire was initially reported at 750 acres and expanded rapidly due to dry conditions, gusty winds, and a large volume of dead timber, particularly in areas infested with spruce budworms. It is believed to have been started by an unattended campfire. The fire moved into the Superior National Forest, causing closures and evacuations. Initial fire behavior included crown fires and rapid spread through dense forest, fueled by widespread dead and dying trees. At least 144 structures, primarily homes and cabins along Highway 44, were destroyed by the fire's initial spread. Initially, mandatory evacuations were put in place for Highway 44 and nearby communities, and evacuation centers were established to assist displaced residents. On Wednesday, May 28, 2025, the the local Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) area forestry assumed management of the Camp House fire. Firefighting operations continued into June with the fire not being 100% contained until the morning of June 13th. The fire reached a maximum size of 12,071 acres and affected around 150 structures.

First of two tornadoes from a severe thunderstorm that crossed through Cass and Crow Wing Counties. The tornado began just north of Casino, Minnesota, and moved northeasterly for about 3.75 miles before taking an easterly turn near the end of Home Brook Lane on the south end of Hardy Lake. It then traveled east-southeast for about 7 miles and crossed into Crow Wing County while over Gull Lake. The tornado continued into Crow Wing County for about three-quarters of a mile moving back on shore then dissipating after crossing Sea Gull Road NW at 1643 CDT. Damage along the path was mainly limited to hardwood and softwood trees that were snapped about 10 to 20 feet up (DI 27/28, DOD 4). Near the beginning of the tornado, it moved across a homestead causing roof damage to the attached garage of a home and pushed the entire unanchored garage structure about one foot (DI 1, DOD 4).

First of two tornadoes from a severe thunderstorm that crossed through Cass and Crow Wing Counties. The tornado began just north of Casino, Minnesota, and crossed into Crow Wing County about 5.25 miles southwest of Lake Hubert while over Gull Lake. The tornado continued into Crow Wing County for about three-quarters of a mile moving back on shore then dissipating after crossing Sea Gull Road NW at 1643 CDT. Damage along the path was mainly limited to hardwood and softwood trees that were snapped about 10 to 20 feet up (DI 27/28, DOD 4).

This is the second of two tornadoes that were observed and produced damage from a severe thunderstorm. The tornado developed along Moody Lane, just east of Crimson Lane, and moved northeast for about 1.5 miles before turning east-southeast near the south end of Mollie Lake. The tornado then tracked east-southeast for about 3.8 miles before turning east-northeast just after crossing Rebel Road. The tornado then continued across the Mississippi River and into Cuyuna Lakes State Park for about 5.6 miles before dissipating along the north shore of Huntington Mine Lake. Damage along the path of this tornado was almost entirely tree damage with hardwood and softwood trees snapped about 10 to 20 feet above the ground (DI 27/28, DOD 4). Extensive tree damage was observed along Sugar Bush Trail North west of Merrifield with the road completely blocked by fallen trees for a time. The maximum width of the tornado was 900 yards near the south end of Mollie Lake.

events.event_narrative: A man was washed into Lake Superior by a wave on the shore near Solbakken Resort in Lutsen, Minnesota. He was walking along the shore and was knocked over by a large wave and pulled out into Lake Superior and was not moving. His body was recovered by United States Border Patrol who responded to a mutual aid call by Cook County Search and Rescue after conditions proved too rough for their boat. Waves were around two to four feet at the time with south-southwesterly winds of 10 to 20 knots with gusts to 25 knots.

Lake effect snowfall of 3 to 6 inches were reported across the county. The heaviest snowfall was in the far eastern and southern parts of the county. A high report of 7 inches was recorded near Butternut.

Lake effect snowfall affected mainly the northern part of the county with accumulations quickly dropping off moving south from the northern border. The heaviest snowfall was in the far northern part of the county where a high report of 7 inches was recorded near Butternut.

Heavy lake effect snowfall across the county resulted in snowfall totals of 4 to 8 inches. Higher amounts were recorded along the Penokee Range where 9 to 12 inches fell. A high report of 12 inches was received from Gile.

A heavy band of lake effect snow set up over Duluth and into the Proctor area the afternoon and evening hours of the 29th. This band was expected to quickly shift to the east, but ended up stalling out over the same area for an extended period of time. This led to snowfall totals of 4 to 6 inches in these areas with a high report of 6.5 inches in the Morgan Park neighborhood of Duluth.

A heavy band of lake effect snow set up over Superior the afternoon and evening hours of the 29th. This band was expected to quickly shift to the east, but ended up stalling out over the same area for an extended period of time. This led to snowfall totals of 4 to 6 inches in town with a high report of 7 inches in the South End neighborhood of Superior.

A band of lake effect moved across the Bayfield Peninsula during the evening and early morning hours of the 29th into the 30th. This band was fairly transient by this point, but was still able to produce some very heavy snowfall in the Cornucopia area. Snowfall totals of 5 to 9 inches were reported in and near Cornucopia with a high report of 9.5 inches about six miles south of town.

In addition to the lake effect snow along the South Shore, an area of low pressure brought snow to parts of inland northwest Wisconsin on the 29th as well. Most of the snowfall totals around Burnett County remained under 6 inches, but the Grantsburg area did receive up to 6.2 inches of accumulation by the time the snow ended during the early morning hours of the 30th.

While the bulk of the snowfall fell to areas south and east of northern St. Louis County, some areas did see some higher amounts. Upwards of 7 inches of accumulation was reported in Ely with this system.
Snowfall totals across Price County were in the 5 to 8 inch range for the event. A high report of 10.6 inches was reported about 6 miles northwest of Butternut.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 7 inches were reported across the Minnesota Arrowhead during the event. A high total of 7.5 inches was recorded about 30 miles northwest of Grand Marias.

Snowfall totals of 5 to 8 inches of heavy wet snow were reported across the southern part of Cook County. A high report of 9 inches was recorded about 4 miles northwest of Grand Marais.

Snowfall totals of 10 to 20 inches were common with a high report of 32.3 inches near Mercer.

The severe storm that produced the tornado tracked northeast along the Saint Croix River Valley on the Minnesota-Wisconsin state border. Although the tornado crossed through mostly recreational land, residents between Rush City and Rock Creek in MN, as well as Grantsburg to Yellow Lake in WI were impacted. The maximum path width was a quarter mile, or 400 yards, with an average path width of 400 to 600 ft. The tornado exited Pine County at around 1955 CST, continuing on in Burnett County, WI, where it lifted at 2001 CST, about 3.5 miles northwest of Grantsburg, WI. The total path length was about 6.5 miles. ||The worst of the damage occurred in far southeast Pine County and was evidence of a strong EF2 tornado with estimated winds of 110-135 mph. This rating was based on the total destruction of a strapped down mobile home and the extensive uprooting/snapping of trees where the tornado crossed Minnesota State Highway 70.  Two people in a mobile home were injured.  Multiple homes sustained significant damage.

This tornado likely began on the southern tip of Big Island. Aerial photographs taken by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources showed evidence of tornado damage on smaller islands over the western part of the flowage between the Turtle Dam and Springstead Landing. These islands had large sections of trees completely destroyed - either snapped or uprooted, and the aerial photographs revealed trees laying across one another in a cross-hatched pattern, in a few cases at 90 degree incidence angles. ||Substantial tree damage began occurring near Springstead Landing and east into a small neighborhood near the intersection of Flowage Rd. and Franks Ln. A stand of large trees between Flowage Landing Rd. and Simmons Rd. was completely demolished with similar evidence of tornadic winds. All of the trees were snapped or uprooted. ||Impacts to cabins in the area started on the western edge of Simmons Rd. and then continued into the neighborhood near the northern tip of Flowage Rd. Some structures in this area were damaged by falling trees. The tree damage in this neighborhood was still rather significant, with large trees up to 2 feet in diameter uprooted or snapped. The tornado then continued east where uprooted and snapped trees were noted along the edge of the shoreline near campsites D-31, C-2, and D-35 before damage became much more sporadic near the canoe portage. It was at this point where the damage path narrowed and the tornado likely ended.  Three campers were injured while camping at remote campsites on the Turtle-Flambeau Flowage.

Some tree damage was noted along County Highway E to the west of Park Falls for approximately 4 miles.
Some tree damage noted near Agenda Road and Woodpecker Lane near the Ashland-Price County border.
There were 12 to 14 inch diameter trees down across Kley Road northwest of Park Falls.

There was minor siding damage to a home, a metal barn collapsed, and some trees were blown down along Balsam Lane to the east-southeast of Butternut. The metal barn probably collapsed at a lower wind speed than would normally be expected, given a lack of damage to nearby pine trees. Estimated wind gusts in this area were around 80 mph.

There was sporadic tree damage from near and east of Butternut to the northeast into the area just northwest of the Turtle Flambeau Flowage. Also, a large volume of hail fell in Butternut. Effects were probably a combination of two severe thunderstorms that tracked over the same area.
Several trees were blown down.
Some small trees and tree branches down near Highway 70/27 intersection.

Large trees were blown down in far southwest Price County.
Several small farm outbuildings were destroyed. Nearby large barns and house only sustained minor damage.
Large tree branches were blown down.

A weak tornado tracked for just over a mile around U.S. Highway 8 to the west of Prentice. The damage was primarily to trees, with a few 6-12 inch diameter pine trees snapped and blown in a convergent damage pattern. A metal barn also had some minor damage, mainly to eaves and siding. [DI 1 (SBO), DOD 1, EXP-UB, Est Gust 70 mph].
A brief, weak tornado occurred north-northwest of Prentice. Only tree damage was noted along the damage path. [DI 28 (TS), DOD 2, EXP, Est Gust 75 mph].

A tornado affected the area near the intersection of County Highway H and Willow Road. A citizen reported a tornado around this location that further corroborates the damage survey findings. Damage along the path was mostly to trees. A small shed was destroyed, a metal barn lost some roof paneling, and several large trees were snapped at one property. [DI 1 (SBO), DOD 2, EXP, Est. Gust 75-80 mph].
Several large trees were blown down.
A brief weak tornado caused some minor tree damage in far northeast Price County. [DI 28 (TS), DOD 2, LB-EXP, Est. Gust 65-70 mph].
Brief funnels observed to be dipping out of a rotating wall cloud.

Some trees and tree limbs blown down in an area between Marble Lake and Kane Lake. This damage was likely associated with a downburst immediately prior to the formation of a tornado just to the east.
Some sporadic minor tree damage was noted along a section of Highway 15. There were some broken large tree limbs, as well as a few trees blown down. This was associated with non-tornadic winds.

Three trees blown down blocking Highway 5 and Perch Lake Road.

A brief tornado occurred in a heavily forested area west of Silver Bay in southern Lake County, roughly along a 2 mile stretch of US Forest Service Road 107 (Kane Lake Road). There were a few pine trees snapped or uprooted, a few ash and birch trees uprooted, and some broken birch tree limbs. The damage seemed to be focused into narrower corridors within the broader tornado path, possibly indicative of smaller vorticies within the overall tornado. This matches well with an eyewitness report that was received of a rotating wall cloud with some small funnels occasionally protruding from the base. No structural damage was observed. [DI 28 (TS), DOD 3, LB-EXP, Est. Gust 70-80 mph].
Several 8-inch diameter trees were blown down about 5 miles west of Sarona on Highway D.
Power lines were blown down.
Trees were blown down.

Trees and power lines were blown down across most county roads between County Highway 11 and the Merrifield area. Many of the trees were healthy and about a foot in diameter. Trees fell on campers at Mission Lake. There was also damage reported to the docks at the east end of Pelican Lake.

This was the corridor of an intense down-burst wind-damage found just west of Danbury.  The corridor was 1/4 mile wide and 500 yards long, within which every single tree was snapped off or flattened.
Widespread wind damage to trees in the Dairyland area, with many homes impacted by falling trees.  One tree fell through the roof of a house.
Many trees were blown down, smashing campers and cars at Red Lake Resort.
This was a corridor of intense down-burst wind damage found just west of Danbury.  Wind speeds were estimated well in excess of 100 mph.

The Red Cross opened a shelter to distribute food and water.  Estimated wind speed is derived from the NWS WFO Duluth Storm Survey.

An eleven year old girl was killed while trying to escape the approaching storm.  Lightning struck a tree and the tree fell on the girl, killing her.  The tree was so large that it took 20 men to remove it.

The rip current suddenly developed about 515 PM CDT when light east winds shifted to west 15 to 20 mph, with gusts 25 to 30 mph.  Wind reports at Duluth International Airport, the Superior WI Bong Airport and the Sky Harbor Airport were used to obtain these directions and speeds.

Overnight rainfall of 2 to 5 inches across Cook County caused downtown Grand Marais to flood.  Five inches of rain fell at Golden Eagle Lodge on the Gunflint Trail while 2.91 inches fell in Grand Marais.Most of the rain fell between 3:00 am and 6: am CDT. Cook County Road 8, also known as Devil Track Road, was flooded as were a few other county roads.
The winds blew down numerous trees. Several homes were damaged from falling trees. There was also some structural damage at the Ashland County fairgrounds.
The intense winds brought down hundreds of trees. A barn was destroyed, a new recreational vehicle camper was destroyed, a home had major roof damage and a beef cow was killed.
The hail shredded 100 acres of corn.

Thunderstorm winds toppled a large tree onto an electrical wire, almost causing a fire.  Also, 1.5 miles west of Stone Lake a large oak tree fell across Highway 70 near Golden Pond Road.  Also, on Lake Road trees were uprooted and went through the roof a  garage and a chicken coop. A 125-year old white pine was uprooted and fell against a home, taking out a dormer.  Power was lost for at least three days. Also, strong winds hit the southeast end of Stone Lake where tree loss was in the hundreds. Many boat lifts on the lake were flipped upside down.

Heavy rains on August 2nd resulted in major flooding of the Nemadji River and the tributary Black River. Many roads were washed out, including Wisconsin State Route 35. Specifically, the Nemadji River Gage, near Superior, reached the flood stage of 20 feet at 1230 PM CDT August 2nd, crested at 27.37 feet at 200 AM CDT August 3rd, and returned back below flood stage at 300 PM CDT August 4th. The crest was the highest ever reported for that gage.

November began with severe drought conditions across western areas, in the Taconite Harbor and Tofte areas.  During November, severe drought conditions spread throughout the entire area.
Severe drought conditions were in the Silver Bay area in early November.  During the month, severe drought conditions spread across the entire area.
Severe drought conditions persisted across eastern areas, including the Ely area.  Moderate drought continued across the rest of the area.

Severe drought areas were east of Cook and south of Ely early in November.  Severe drought spread throughout the eastern part of the Iron Range by the end of the month.  Moderate drought continued throughout the rest of the area.

River flooding continued from heavy rains in May 2012, with a crest of 15.09 feet on June 1st.  The river fell below the 12 foot flood stage at 400 PM CST on June 12th.

River flooding continued from heavy late May rain.  The Mississippi River reached a long-lasting crest of 14.59 feet at the Brainerd gauge on June 2nd, 1.59 feet above the flood stage of 13 feet.  The river returned to flood stage at 400 AM June 8th.

The month began with the Mississippi River above flood stage at the Fort Ripley gauge due to heavy rains during May. June began with the river cresting at 11.70 ft or 1.70 feet above flood stage.  The river gauge went missing with the river still 10.40 feet, 0.40 feet above the 10 foot flood stage near midnight the night of June 6th.  The gauge returned to service at 200 PM on June 13th showing the river below flood stage.
Big Sandy Lake remained above the 1218.3 foot ASL flood stage from heavy May rains.  The lake crested at 800 AM June 4th and fell below flood stage June 12th at 600 AM.
Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 to 60 mph brought down six-inch diameter branches.
Trees, some 5 to 16 inches in diameter, were blown down.

The Nemadji River gage, at Superior, normally between 4 and 5 feet, rose to 20 feet early in the morning of June 20th.  The river reached a record stage of 27.91 feet at 100 AM on June 21st, then fell back below 20 feet about midnight the night of June 22nd.  Most of the runoff, resulting in the high stages, came from excessively heavy rain on Carlton County MN flowing downstream. Many roads were flooded in Superior and surrounding areas from the flood of the river and the excessive rainfall.  Many buildings at he University of Wisconsin in Superior (UWS) was flooded. Uninsured damage at UWS was $8-10 million. Damage to homes was estimated at $6.3 million. Damage to businesses was estimated at $4 million.
Several large trees were blown down.
A twelve-inch diameter tree was blown down.
An 8 inch diameter tree was uprooted and a 6 inch diameter tree was snapped off three feet above the ground.
Large trees were blown down along West Shore Road.
A ten-inch diameter tree blew over and brought down a power line.
The Little Cloquet River rose rapidly and was at the base of the bridge over Pequaywan Lake Road.  The river rose about a foot in 12 hours.
Fox Farm Road was washed out near the intersection of Pequaywan Lake Road. It was also washed out two miles east of that intersection.
The wind was measured at Blatnik Bridge, near Pier 20, in Duluth.
Low -lying areas and curb to curb road flooding occurred.
Many roads are flooded and impassable in town.
The downtown area was flooded where 4 to 6 inches of water covered roadways.
Arrowhead Road, between Haines and Arlington roads, was flooded.
Two inches of water covered Superior Street in downtown Duluth.
Deepening water covered roadways around Woodland and St Marie Avenues.
Water covered the eastbound lane at Highway 194 and US Highway 53.
The first southbound tunnel on Interstate 35 in Duluth was flooded and impassable.
Brewer Creek overflowed onto 3rd Street between 6th Avenue East and 7th Avenue East. There are 4 inches of water on the roadway and considerable debris.

Six to 10 inches of rain fell overnight on the 19th and during the following day, resulting in stream and river flooding. Many driveways were washed out. The Knife River flooded Highway 61 and resulted in evacuations in the town of Knife River. Other smaller state and county roads were washed out.  Water was flowing across Highway 61 on the northeast end of Two Harbors.
Water was over the road at Washington Street.  Other roads in the area were also flooded.

There was six inches of water over Highway 61 at the junction with Highway 1 due to the flooding of the west branch of the Baptism River. There was also significant flooding of the golf course at Beaver bay and of Rockwood Road at Silver Bay, due to flooding of the Beaver River and Palisade River, respectively.
Water covered a large area of road at Highway 53 and Maple Grove Road making that area impassable and flooding many businesses due to the flooding from Miller Creek and urbanization.

Numerous roads were washed out and flooded throughout Duluth. This flooding included several large sink holes and collapsed roads. There were large numbers of high-water rescues and evacuations across the city.
The White Pine River flooded onto Highway 33, with three feet of water covering the roadway.
Maple Grove Road, about a mile east of Midway Road, was under at least three feet of water from the flooded Midway River.
Deep water covered the road at 57th Avenue West from the flooded Keene Creek. Irving Park was completely under water and many homes in the Irving Park area were flooded.

Martin Road, between Lavaque Road and Rice Lake Road, was under water due to flooding of Miller Creek.  Downstream, the Miller Creek flooded many businesses in the Mall area, including Target a large restaurant and parts of the Miller Hill Mall. The mall was closed for two days.

Jay Cooke State Park was evacuated due to severe flooding  of the St. Louis River.|Highway 210 through the park was heavily damage. The historic swinging pedestrian bridge was washed away. Miles of hiking and biking trails were damaged.

The reservoir at the City of Thomson overflowed and Carlton County Emergency Management ordered the evacuation of Thomson. Most of the town was flooded. The water remained for many days. Many homes were lost or severely damaged.
In Midway Township, the Midway River nearly washed out the bridge at Midway Road.
Roadways were completely under water at Pacific Avenue and Exeter Street.
The bridge in North Cloquet, at Midway River was washed out. Local railroads were no longer usable.
Much of Ridge Road was washed out due to St. Louis River flooding.
The St. Louis River and Floodwood River flooded many streets in Floodwood. Law Enforcement ordered the evacuation of several houses on 4th and 5th Avenues.
The center of town was under 1.5 to 2 feet of water due to the flooding of the St. Louis River.
Three inch diameter tree limbs were blown down.

Flooding began at 1100 PM CST, June 17th as the Mississippi River rose to the flood stage of 12 feet.  The river crested at 18.72 feet at 600 PM CST on June 29th, and ended the month above flood stage at 18.42 feet.

The Mississippi River, at Brainerd, rose to its flood stage of 13 feet at 500 AM CST on June 20th, rising to a record-breaking crest of 17.61 feet at 11:30 AM CST on June 28th.  The Mississippi River ended the month at 17.48 feet, which was well above flood stage and also nearly a foot above the previous record stage.

The Mississippi River at Fort Ripley rose to its 10 foot flood stage at 11:00 PM CST June 19th.  The Mississippi River crested at 12.42 feet at 8:00 AM CST on June 25th.  The river remained at 11.68 feet, above flood stage, through the end of June.  As a result of the Mississippi River flooding, many tributaries became backed up and flooded.  Parts of Crow Wing State Park were flooded, included the picnic areas, trails and the boat landing. The boat landing was reopened on July 24th.  The Black Bear and Miller Lakes neighborhoods was flooded. Numerous roads and bridges were damaged across Crow Wing County.

The gage at Big Sandy Lake reached its flood stage of 1218.30 feet ASL at 8:00 AM CST on June 20th.  The lake crested at 1222.93 feet ASL at 1100 PM CST on June 26th.  Big Sandy Lake remained above flood stage, at 1222.73 feet ASL at the end of June.

Flooding of the St Louis River began at the Scanlon gage at 1:30 AM CST on June 20th when it reached a level of 10.50 feet.  The St Louis River reached a record-breaking crest of 16.66 feet at 3 am CST on June 21.  The St Louis River returned below its flood stage of 10.50 feet on June 28th at 10:00 AM CST. Businesses and a campground near the river were flooded.

The Kettle River crested at a record-breaking stage of 18.0 feet from 11:00 PM CST on June 21st through 5:00 AM CST on June 22nd.  The Kettle River returned to a 10 foot stage on June 25th at noon CST.

The tornado formed 2 miles south-southwest of Deerwood, MN and traveled southeast across Nokay Lake Road where 2 mobile homes were destroyed.  There were three residents of the mobile home- a mother, father and young son. The mother and father received non-life-threatening injuries. The tornado continued to move southeast over Placid Lake. Several mature hardwood trees were snapped approximately 5 feet above ground level on the west side of the lake indicating another area of EF2 damage. Additional EF2 tree damage was observed as the tornado moved onshore along the southeast side of Placid Lake. Extensive tree damage was observed along a stretch of MN-6, at a summer camp, and over portions of a golf course. The tornado weakened beyond the golf course and dissipated before reaching Tame Fish Lake Road.

A 79-year-old man with medical complications died in his trailer home during a heat wave. The cause of death was listed as cardiac arrhythmia secondary to dehydration. He had a history of hypertension, which was treated with medication, and he was a smoker. He had a syncopal episode one month prior to his death when sitting at picnic table by his trailer home. He had been working on window replacements and remodeling the interior. The following day he went to the emergency department for work up, was found to be mildly dehydrated. ||The trailer home he was working on is located in the Kimball Township of Iron County Wisconsin. The date of death was July 8, 2016. He was found July 9, 2016. The exact time of death is unknown, but thought to be late afternoon. There was a single small room fan running in the trailer. ||The heat was a contributing factor along with insufficient ventilation and proper re-hydration.

The tornado developed in a wooded area and bog in far northern Aitkin County, about 1.25 miles north-northeast of the intersection of Highways 65 and 200. The tornado tracked northeast and continued into Itasca County.  The tornado moved through far southeast Itasca County, crossing US Highway 2 and dissipating near a grove of trees approximately 1 mile west of the St. Louis County line. The tornado destroyed several pole barns, lofted a roof from a house, and destroyed the house. Analysis of the construction methods at this location, and surrounding damage, yielded a rating of EF-0. However, EF-1 tree damage was noted immediately west and north of Sabo 2 and continued eastward. The tornado reached its maximum intensity approximately 2.2 miles southwest of Wawina where high-end EF-1 damage was noted to a stand of trees. Oblique angle aerial photography from the western end of the track revealed a path through the bog adjacent to US-2, which was not directly observable from the air nor from the ground. The tornado moved through two small stands of trees breaking branches and snapping a few narrow trunks before dissipating. Several videos and photographs of this tornado have been reported.

The tornado developed east of the Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad near the St. Louis River and tracked east-northeast for approximately 3.1 miles while producing sporadic pockets of low-end EF1 damage to softwood trees. The tornado struck a house which resulted in partial uplift of the roof and lofting of roofing materials. The tornado also flattened a decorative windmill and bent a flagpole. The roofing material was distributed downwind to a range of 380 yards. The tornado also snapped and uprooted several trees in this vicinity. The damage at this location was also rated EF-1. The sporadic damage track continued for another mile to the east-northeast. There was a distinct weakening of the tornado with several pockets of broken branches and limbs noted approximately 3 miles southwest of Zim. The tornado then turned southeast and the damage track tightened once again with a wide swath of EF-0 tree damage and pockets of low-end EF-1 damage. The sporadic EF-1 damage continued as the tornado crossed MN-7 and dissipated southwest of Stone Lake.

There were heat index readings around or slightly over 100 degrees across Pine County. The St. Croix RAWS reached 105 degrees, the Hinckley AWOS reached 103 degrees, and the Minnesota Department of Transportation's RWIS near Rutledge reached 100 degrees.

The Pine River AWOS reached only 92 degrees, but there were readings of 95 to 100 degrees just east of the Cass County border in Crow Wing County.

While there were no heat index readings of 95 to 100 degrees specifically within northern Cass County, there were nearby readings of 95 to 100 degrees in nearby southern Itasca County (the Grand Rapids AWOS reached 95 degrees), northern Aitkin County (the Hill City AWOS reached 99 degrees), and Crow Wing County (the Emily RWIS reached 97 degrees). Therefore, it looks like southeastern parts of northern Cass County, probably near Outing and Remer, likely reached 95 to 100 degrees.

The Duluth ASOS and a weather station in Esko only reached 93 degrees. The RWIS along Interstate 35 near Otter Creek and Atkinson reached a whopping 115 degrees, but it seems like such an outlier compared to all the other readings that it seems too suspicious to consider accurate.

An elderly couple were found dead from exposure to the cold weather in a remote part of Superior, Wisconsin. A utility worker found Richard Ellison, 82, and Shirley Johnson, 70, on their deck around 10:30 am on Wednesday December 21st. They were last seen running errands the previous Sunday, December 18th. It appeared the couple misplaced their house keys and were unable to get into their home. The nearest neighbor was a half-block away, but few people live in that part of town. It was unclear why the couple did not seek shelter in their vehicle or attempt to seek help at their neighbor's home. It was particularly cold on Sunday into early Monday, with the recorded high temperature on Sunday being only 1 degree, and the Monday morning low temperature -8 degrees. It warmed up significantly the rest of the week with high temperatures in the 30s and lows in the teens to round 20 degrees.

A sheriff deputy was rescued from Twentymile Creek near Mason, WI after he mistakenly drove his vehicle into a washed-out section of road caused by heavy rainfall across the region. The deputy clung to a tree using an emergency tourniquet to keep from being swept away. It took emergency personnel close to 4 hours to rescue the deputy. The deputy was rushed to the hospital where he was hospitalized for kidney failure and other life-threatening problems associated with clinging to the tree in the flood waters. The deputy has since made a full recovery and returned to duty later that month.

A supercell thunderstorm tracked across northwest Wisconsin during the late afternoon and early evening of 5/16/2017. The storm produced a strong, 83-mile-long track tornado which affected 4 Wisconsin counties (Polk, Barron, Rusk, and Price). The tornado developed at 4:42 pm over southeastern Polk County, east of Clear Lake, then moved east-northeastward across southern Barron County, and then east across southern Rusk counties into southwest Price County. The tornado tore across the Prairie Lake Estate 50-unit mobile home park halfway between Chetek and Cameron in Barron County. Dozens of mobile homes were destroyed and damaged from high-end EF-2 wind speeds. About a couple dozen people were injured, one seriously, and one adult man lost his life. The most intense damage was north of the Village of Conrath in Rusk County. A family home was completely destroyed down to the foundation, which resulted in an EF rating of 3 (140 mph). The remainder of the tornado's path ranged from EF0 to EF1 with mainly tree damage and occasional structural damage. The damage in Price County, along the last miles of its track, was EF0. The tornado dissipated at 7:10 pm. The tornado lasted 2 hours and 28 minutes.||As of June 2017, this was Wisconsin's longest tracked tornado on record since modern National Weather Service tornado records were established in 1950.

A supercell thunderstorm developed east of Zim, MN at 3:40 PM CDT and moved initially northeast, but quickly turned easterly, taking on supercell characteristics by 4:00 PM CDT. A tornado developed at 4:25 PM CDT one-quarter mile northwest of Moilan Lake and uprooted several trees on the northwest shore and continuing to the northeast shore. Damage at the start of the track was rated EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 80 mph. The tornado initially tracked southeastward and turned easterly over a homestead on the southeast shore of the lake. Numerous mature softwood trees were uprooted and some trees were broken near the base. Winds near the homestead were estimated between 85 and 90 mph, with the intensity increasing to low-end EF-1. The tornado continued to break and uproot mature trees as it traveled eastward and crossed Moilan Road. The tornado reached peak intensity as it traveled through a stand of trees one-quarter miles east of Moilan Road. Numerous trees were broken near their base. Winds at this location were estimated between 90 and 95 mph, still an EF-1 tornado. The tornado continued eastward and began to weaken crossing Tavern Road and turning northeast. Several trees were broken and uprooted near Tavern Road with estimated winds between 80 and 95 mph. The tornado moved across two homesteads east of Tavern Road as it was weakening and dissipated at 4:31 PM CDT after crossing Pond Road, approximately three-tenths of a mile east of the intersection with Tavern Road.

Onshore waves and strong winds off of Lake Superior pummeled the shoreline around Duluth throwing rocks and upending concrete-based walkways. Portions of the the Duluth Lakewalk, Brighton Beach, Canal Park, and Park Point were damaged. A disaster declaration was authorized by Minnesota Governor Mark Dayton for $2.12 million from the state and $1.38 million from the local governments totaling $3.5 million for repairs and cleanup. $2.5 million in damage was just in the city of Duluth alone with damage found also along Scenic Highway 61.

Lightning struck a cabin just north of the Brainerd International Raceway. It went through the roof and struck a 15 year-old boy who was lying in bed before passing through the boxspring of the bed and exiting the cabin through an electrical outlet. The boy received  superficial injuries. The bed he was on started on fire and there was damage to the electrical system of the cabin and an air conditioner.

Lightning struck a tree in Big Bay Town Park. The current then traveled through the root system and struck a woman getting into her vehicle, throwing her to the ground. Two men in a tent next to the tree were also struck. The woman and one of the men had minor injuries, but the other man sustained serious burns and was transported off the island for medical treatment.
There were several reports of trees and power lines blown down in Duluth.
An 8 inch diameter tree was blown down near the intersection of US Highway 53 and MN Highway 194.

Environment Canada conducted a survey of the long-tracked tornado, which began and mostly occurred in Ontario before crossing into Minnesota, and rated the damage on their end as EF-2, and as EF-1 on the short distance in Minnesota before it dissipated. Satellite imagery is available to show the clear path of the tornado. The total path length was about 8.5 miles, only 0.9 miles of which occurred in Minnesota.
The hail lasted about 10 minutes.

Lac Coutre Oreilles Emergency Management reported numerous trees down with many being 8 to 12 inches in diameter. Three of the trees fell onto structures and cars. The bulk of the trees fell south of the Junction of Froemel and Trepania Roads. Damage photos are indicative of a microburst.
Strong thunderstorm winds blew over an oak tree onto an occupied camper, killing one of the occupants and injuring 3 others. Numerous trees were blown over roadways in the area as well.

A landspout tornado developed in a shower in the Fish Lake Wildlife Area. The location was approximated by triangulating features from the many photographs of the tornado, talking to the witnesses, and using Google satellite and street view tools. It was not readily possibly to conduct a storm survey to determine its path (it was likely short) and its strength because of the inaccessibility of the area.
The Delta-Drummond Road was completely washed out near Drummond. Over 15 inches or rain was recorded in Drummond over the previous 48 hours, with much of it falling over the previous 6 to 12 hours.
Multiple roads were reported washed out in the Summit and Dairyland areas, including a 3+ mile stretch of State Highway 35.
County Highway A was closed between Solon Springs and Amnicon Lake due to water over the road.

Wisconsin Highway 13 was flooded between US Highway 2 and Cherryville Road. Water had overflowed from both Whittlesey Creek and Fish Creek.

The observer recorded 1.43 inches of rainfall in 40 minutes which led to water over the roads on their farm. A seasonal creek on the property was estimated to be running at 15 times its capacity. Water was 6 inches over the road between fields.

Denver Road was closed due to water over topping the road from the adjacent Ounce River. The spotter reported 7.9 inches of rain between 9:30 PM the evening of the 16th through 4:30 PM on the 17th. Multiple trees were down in the area as well.
Water was flowing over Knight Road were it crosses the Gile Flowage.

A truck went into a ditch on County Truck E just south of County Trunk C in the Township of White River. The roadway was completely underwater and the water in the ditch was 6 to 8 feet in depth. The truck was found unoccupied with the driver side door open. The 75 year old male driver was found deceased 60 feet from the vehicle.
A bridge over south Fish Creek was damaged on US Highway 63 just south of US Highway 2. Both US 2 and US 63 were closed due to cars driving onto flooded roadways and becoming stranded.
