Floodwaters washed out a stone culvert on the BNSF Railway railroad tracks, opening up a 300' long and 60' deep hole in the railroad roadbed. The tracks were suspended over the washout. A new steel culvert was built and the tracks were returned to service at midnight on June 22nd.
Local officials report water over all downstream bridges from the Radigan Dam on the Tamarack River, indicating it had been breached.

The Namadji River experienced record flooding, reaching a crest of 29.5 feet at the SOSW3 gauge on the south side of Superior. The previous record crest was 27.4 feet. This led to numerous road closures in Superior due to flooding with the most significant road closed being US Highway 2 between 31st Ave East and 37th Ave East where the road crosses the river shortly before it empties into Allouez Bay.
Whittlesley Creek reached a record stage at 6:50PM on the 17th when it hit 7.52 feet. This breaks the old record of 7.3 feet set on June 21, 2013.
The White River near Ashland set a record crest reaching 9.91 feet at 9AM June 17th. This broke the previous record crest of 8.54 feet set on July 12th, 2016.

The St. Croix River near Danbury set a record stage of 11.66 feet at 12:30PM on June 18th. This beat the old record of 8.72 feet set April 24th, 2001. Due to this flooding, Wisconsin Highway 35, which is where the gauge is located, was closed.

events.event_narrative: A family of five (husband, wife, three children under the age of 10) set out on a kayak to tour the Apostle Islands at around 100 pm CDT. Wind and waves were nearly calm when the family set out from Madeline Island on a sit on top type of kayak. The winds picked up by 4 pm becoming east-southeast at 5-15 mph with waves building to 1-3 feet, causing the kayak to overturn, sending the family into the water.  All occupants were wearing life jackets, however, water temperatures were around 60 degrees and they were not wearing wet suits. The father and children tried to swim to the nearest island while the mother remained with the boat. She had a cell phone and tried to text for help, but cell coverage was poor. A text message from the mother went through around 8:30 pm to her sister, who then contacted police. Search teams were deployed and the wife was found alive just after 10 pm. The father and two of the children were found deceased after midnight on the 31st and the third child was found deceased at about 10 am the same day. The cause of death of the father and children was hypothermia due to the 60 degree water.

The tornado began at 654 PM CDT just east of Rusk Road and north of US Highway 8 in a wooded area and moved toward the east-southeast. The tornado crossed Midway Road east of Woodlawn Road to the west-southwest of Catawba and flipped a chicken coop and removed a roof from an outbuilding. It then continued east-southeast and crossed County Road I between Main Street and Moonshine Alley where a farmstead lost shingles off a single family home and several trees were damaged. The tornado began east of the intersection of Sand Road and Cabin Lane. The damage path was picked up the where it crossed Cabin Lane several hundred yards west of Sand Road.  Numerous uprooted and broken softwood trees were noted on either side of Cabin Lane at that location. The damage at that location was consistent with high-end EF-0 wind speeds of 75 to 85 mph. The tornado continued east-southeast and strengthened to EF-1 intensity south of the intersection of Sand Road and Cabin Lane. Extensive tree damage was noted with nearly all trees in the area broken or uprooted. This damage seemed consistent with winds of 85 to 95 mph. From that location to a point just west of Schaefer Road a path was cut through the trees which was approximately 80 yards wide and approximately one-half mile in length. All the trees in this area were either broken or uprooted and the damage was consistent with winds of 100 to 110 mph. The tornado weakened quickly after crossing Schaefer Road. A few broken branches and uprooted trees were noted along Jackson Road and locations farther east. It seems the tornado lifted between Schaefer Road and Jackson Road, which is where the end of the track was approximated.

A damage survey of a tornado within Voyageurs National Park has |been completed and confirmed a tornado from approximately Locator |Lake, approximately 6.4 miles north of Kabetogama, to Marion Bay |on Rainy Lake, approximately 9.2 miles north-northeast of |Kabetogama. The tornado likely extended farther northeast across |Rainy Lake and possibly into Canada, so the length of this tornado|should be considered an estimate. The end point location is |estimated from video of the tornado moving over Rainy Lake. This |survey was completed using photos and videos from Voyageurs |National Park, the public, and business owners in the region. Very|special thanks to Voyageurs National Park for sharing aerial |images of the damage path which was critical to assessing the |path, width, and severity of this tornado.

The supercell which produced the Gheen Hill tornado began north |of Togo in far southeast Koochiching County. It traveled toward |the east-northeast and gradually organized. Sporadic straight-line|wind damage was observed a few miles northwest of Gheen and west |of US Highway 53. The tornado developed 1 mile west of US-53 and |tracked toward the east-northeast. We received several photographs|from a spotter who observed the tornado north of Gheen Hill |before it crossed US-53. The tornado crossed Rice Lake and |strengthened to low-end EF-1 intensity shortly after. The tornado |continued east-northeastward across the easternmost portion of |Johnson Road. It weakened and dissipated just to the east of an |ATV trail northwest of Gheen. Aside from the few spotter photos of|this tornado, high-resolution satellite imagery was critical to |assessing the location, path, width, and peak intensity of this |tornado. We are very grateful to the spotter who provided the only|known photos of this tornado. Additional help in identifying this|tornado's path was provided by a private sector meteorologist from Grand|Rapids, MN. This supercell thunderstorm would go on to produce |the Carlson Lake tornado.

The supercell which produced the Gheen Hill tornado continued to |move toward the east-northeast and a second mesocyclone developed |a short time after the Gheen Hill tornado dissipated. The Carlson |Lake tornado developed approximately 500 yards west of the Elbow |River and six-tenths of a mile north of the western end of Ban |Lake. The tornado tracked toward the northeast producing sporadic |EF-0 damage to trees. The tornado turned due east approximately |one mile west of Carlson Lake and intensified. The tornado produced|a swath of EF-1 damage, which was a maximum of 300 yards wide and|passed over Carlson Lake. Tree damage corresponding to high-end |EF-1 wind speeds was noted over much of this area. The tornado |turned toward the northeast after crossing Carlson Lake and |crossed over Elbow Lake Forest Road before gradually weakening. |The tornado dissipated shortly after crossing Shuster Road. We are|very grateful for the help identifying this tornado's path |provided by a private meteorologist in Grand Rapids, MN. High-|resolution satellite imagery was critical to assessing the |location, path, width, and peak intensity of this tornado.

events.event_narrative: A prolonged period of northeast winds led to 2 to 4 foot waves at the head of Lake Superior. Winds were on the downward trend the morning of the 30th with gusts to around 22mph in thundershowers that moved through earlier in the morning, with rain ending around 10AM. Three boaters in aboard a 21 foot Monark Aluminum Hulled boat departed from Superior Bay and entered Lake Superior through the Superior Entry when they turned northwest to parallel Minnesota Point. Waves caused the engine to be overcome with water, and subsequent large waves turned the boat, later flipping it upside down in the water. The boat capsized around 11AM, sending the the occupants into the water. All were wearing life jackets, but they were not zipped up. Two of the boaters reached the shore safely, but the third occupant did not and his body was recovered by the Duluth Fire Department. A Small Craft Advisory was in effect at the time along with a Beach Hazards Statement citing a high risk for rip currents in the area.

Marginally severe storms moved through the area during the early afternoon hours leading to sporadic downed trees. Following the storms, a homeowner was on his roof removing a downed tree when he lost his footing and fell approximately 20 feet to the ground and landing on a propane tank. The closest observing site to the location of the fatality was the Ely Airport which reported a max gust to 30 mph during the storm, but higher gusts were likely based on the tree damage reports.

Conditions were so dangerous, plows were pulled off the roads until the next morning.

Docks were damaged at this location along with a few boats flipped and tree damage. The waterspout then turned more easterly and moved across Church Camp Bay before reaching shore again, damaging another dock, flipping multiple boats and causing sporadic tree damage. It then turned a but more southeasterly and traveled through a grove of trees and dissipated before reaching US Highway 169.

This flooding cut off access to multiple homes and caused damage to roadways. Additionally, bridge damage was reported to an ATV trail and to the Birkebeiner ski trail at the crossings of Mosquito Brook. No damage was reported to any buildings or homes. Roads remained closed into the 28th before water receded.

A weak, brief tornado formed along a line of thunderstorms that moved across Douglas County between 1:00 AM and 2:00 AM CDT. Meteorologists were tracking a number of weak areas of rotation on radar as these storms moved through, and a Tornado Warning was issued for one such area of rotation at 1:10 AM CDT including Maple and Blueberry. At 1:43 AM CDT, meteorologists saw a dramatic increase in radar-detected rotation from this storm just south of Maple, WI, and based on this information issued an additional Tornado Warning using radar-confirmed tornado language to indicate the|confidence in a tornado occurring or imminent. Minutes later, a tornado developed north of Maple and Blueberry knocking down dozens of trees, including snapping some trees off near the base. Just as soon as it developed, the area of rotation weakened|considerably. Radar indicates this tornado may have begun a few minutes earlier but at this time there is not enough conclusive damage evidence that the tornado formed earlier than documented.

A 20-year-old woman was swept 200 yards away from shore at Park Point Beach by a rip current. Duluth Fire Department responded and were able to rescue her. She was sent to the hospital after the rescue in good condition.

Four teenagers were caught in a rip current after conditions quickly changed along Park Point. Temperatures had earlier been in the upper 90s with light westerly winds before the lake breeze pushed inland and dropped temperatures over 30 degrees in 20 minutes as winds turned easterly at about 20 mph. This led to 4 to 6 foot waves at the beach and rip currents. Two women were able to get back to shore while a man attempted to help another teenager when they were separated. That man was able to return to shore by the other teenager was swept 100 yards out by the rip current and was rescued by the Duluth Fire Department and St. Louis County Rescue Squad.

Rescuers responded to the report of a woman who was struggling 40 feet from shore and yelling for help off Park Point Beach on the afternoon of the 1st. The 19-year-old woman was playing in the waves with her friends when a wave knocked her over and she was unable to stand back up and being pulled away from shore. When crews arrived the woman���s friends had been able to get her to the water���s edge. The woman was taken off the beach with the assistance of the Duluth Fire Department then transported to a local hospital for treatment.

On the morning of July 19, 2021, between 10 and 10:30am CDT, a line of sub-severe thunderstorms caused a canoe with two occupants to capsize. Neither were wearing life jackets and one of the two occupants drowned. The incident occurred on Loon Lake east of Crane Lake, Minnesota, within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW). Estimated wind speeds along the line of storms were 25-30 mph based on nearby observations.

Four family members visiting the Hayward area from southern Wisconsin were golfing at the Big Fish Golf Club the morning of the tenth. Storms were developing in the area at that time and one of these storms produced a lightning bolt that hit near the 5th hole's tee box where the four were standing. All four were taken to an area hospital for treatment and were alert when first responders arrived. Two were released that day while the other two remained in the hospital for an unknown length of time. All four of the victims were male and their ages were 14, 19, 38, and 72.

Twin 3-year-old boys were reported missing around 5:30PM the afternoon of the 9th in Hibbing, Minnesota. Officers and neighbors searched for the boys who were located around 6:30PM locked inside a vehicle. Both of the boys were unresponsive and in medical distress when found. Air temperatures at the time were in the middle 80s, but inside the car it was in excess of 120F. One of the boys was airlifted to a children's specialty hospital in Minneapolis, Minnesota, where he later died. The other boy was treated and released from a local hospital.

Two men went canoeing on Sand Lake near Britt, Minnesota, during the afternoon of the 12th. Strong west-northwest winds of 15 to 20 mph with gusts of 25 to 30 mph generated waves on Sand Lake that began to flood the canoe. Both men tried to swim for shore and one made it to an island and was rescued. The other man did not reach land and is presumed to have drowned as they were not wearing life jackets. Rescuers continued to search for the man's body into the weekend.

A wildfire was first detected around 3pm on August 5, 2021, near Greenwood Lake, which is about 15 miles southwest of Isabella. Officials believe the fire was started by a lightning strike in the past that caused a peat bog to smolder. Strong southerly winds and dry conditions on the 5th caused the fire to quickly grow upscale and was affecting around 1,000 acres by the end of the 5th. The fire doubled in size by the 7th to around 2,000 acres and evacuations were in place near the fire. Numerous aircraft were brought in to fight the fire along with ground crews. The fire grew to around 3,000 acres by the 19th and then to nearly 5,000 acres by the 20th. By the 21st, it had grown to over 9,000 acres in size and led to additional evacuations. The US Forest Service also took the rare step of closing the entirety of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness on the 21st for at least a week due to numerous fires in or near the area and the forecast for continued dry and windy conditions. Favorable weather conditions reduced the fire size to 8800 acres on the 22nd before growing to 10,500 acres on the 23rd. The first reports of structures being impacted by the fire were received on the 23rd as well with 14 homes/cabins and 57 outbuildings destroyed. Extreme fire behavior was observed on the 24th with the development of a pyrocumulus cloud and fire-created lightning. The fire increased in size to 19,500 acres on the 24th and increased further to 26,000 acres by the 26th. Cooler temperatures, lighter winds and rainfall arrived on the 27th and 28th allowing crews to reach 14% containment by the morning of the 28th. 1 to 2 of rainfall fell in the area of the fire the night of the 28th into the 29th. Favorable weather conditions the last two days of the month brought containment up to 37% on the 31st.

Fortunately, the lightning strike did not start a fire at the church.

A wildfire was first detected around 3pm on August 5, 2021, near Greenwood Lake in Lake County. Officials believe the fire was started by a lightning strike in the past that caused a peat bog to smolder. The fire was 37% contained at the start of the month and containment increased to around 49% by the 7th thanks to firefighting efforts and around three-quarters of an inch of rainfall. The middle of the month saw around 3 inches of rainfall which helped get containment up to around 80% by the 20th. At this point, the fire was considered well-managed and evacuees were allowed to return to the area. The fire was largely extinguished by the end of the month outside of a few lingering hot spots. The fire burned just under 27,000 acres with the worst day being August 23rd when rapid fire growth resulted in the loss of 14 primary structures and 57 outbuildings. Little to no further losses to buildings were sustained thanks to fire suppression efforts. All remaining fire restrictions across National Forest lands and the BWCWA were lifted on September 17th. The only remaining closures to public lands were in the immediate vicinity of the fire by the end of the month.

While the area of D2 Severe Drought did not change significantly through the month, the southern part of the county did worsen to D0 Abnormally Dry with the update on the 5th. No further changes were observed across the county with the subsequent updates for October.

Drought conditions across Ashland County ranged from None in the far southern portion of the county to D2 Severe Drought around Chequamegon Bay and into the Apostle Islands to begin the month. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches were observed over the month which is about an inch or so below normal. While the area of D2 Severe Drought did not change significantly through the month, the southern part of the county did worsen to D0 Abnormally Dry with the update on the 5th. No further changes were observed across the county with the subsequent updates for October.

Drought conditions across Iron County ranged from None in the far southern portion of the county to D2 Severe Drought adjacent to Lake Superior to begin the month. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches were observed over the month which is about an inch or so below normal. While the area of D2 Severe Drought did not change significantly through the month, the southern part of the county did worsen to D0 Abnormally Dry with the update on the 5th. No further changes were observed across the county with the subsequent updates for October.
A search and rescue crew in the area had to take cover near Eagle Mountain due to the large hail.
A tree was downed onto a power line near the Kabetogama Visitor Center during the storm.
Multiple trees were downed along County Highway 57 on the north side of Devil Track Lake by the storm.
Multiple trees were down along Ball Club Road from the storm.

A rare late-season strong tornado caused tree damage|across parts of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in |northern Cook County. The tornado appeared to begin on Alder Lake, |initially causing damage near Campsite #3 where a small swath of |trees were downed, several snapped halfway down their trunks. The |tornado then traveled north causing sporadic damage until just north |of Rocky Lake where there was a more concentrated area of downed |trees roughly 270 yards across. Sporadic tree damage continued until |reaching Clearwater Lake and crossing the lake just west of Campsite |#5, causing significant damage north of Clearwater Lake and north to |the International Border (Mountain Lake). Significant tree damage was|observed along the Border Route Trail, of which passage was made |impossible as the tornado reached its maximum width of around 500 |yards as it moved across the trail. Numerous trees were snapped near |their bases within this area of damage. The coverage of damage was |widespread with satellite imagery depicting over 80% of trees |uprooted, bent, or snapped across its path near the Border Route |Trail. The tornado then crossed the International Border and continued into Northwestern Ontario, Canada. No private property was damaged along the course of the tornado. ||The National Weather Service appreciates the public reports, photos,|and videos of this tornado damage, aerial photographs from the US |Forest Service, and satellite imagery shared by the Northern |Tornadoes Project (Western University in Canada) which all aided in |an accurate assessment of the damage.

events.event_narrative: Heavier than expected snow led to snow and ice covered roads along the Iron Range. This lead to a multi-vehicle accident near Gilbert that resulted in two fatalities (indirect) and at least two injuries (indirect) from one vehicle. The occupants of the other vehicles in the wreck were not injured or had non-life threatening injuries. Snowfall totals of 5 to 7 inches were reported along the Range with the highest report being 6.8 in Chisholm.
A strong storm brought heavy snow to much of the county in a span of just over 12 hours. Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were reported with the highest report being 8 inches near Big Falls.
Heavier than expected snow was observed across the northern portion of St. Louis County with 6 to 8 inches being reported over a 24-hour period. This highest total was 8 inches near Celina.
While most of the reports around Douglas County were in the 3 to 5 range, the northern part of the county did see some lake enhancement with a report of 6.3 near Poplar.

A vehicle traveling northbound on US 53 near Eveleth lost control on the icy road and went through the median and into the southbound lanes. One of the people in the vehicle was killed (indirect) with two others in the vehicle sustaining non-life threatening injuries.

Drought conditions across Bayfield County ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought across the Bayfield Peninsula to the Chequamegon Bay area to begin the month. Rainfall totals up to around a half inch above normal were in the northern third of the county with totals up to around a half inch below normal across the southern two thirds of the county. D1 Moderate Drought spread across the remainder of the county with no change in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 2nd. No additional changes in the drought status were observed through the remainder of the month.

Drought conditions across Ashland County ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought near Chequamegon Bay to begin the month. Rainfall totals up to around a half inch above normal were observed in the far northeastern corner and much of the southeastern corner of the county with totals up to around a half inch below normal across the remainder of the county. D1 Moderate Drought spread across the remainder of the county with no change in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 2nd. No additional changes in the drought status were observed through the remainder of the month.

Drought conditions across Ashland County ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the far southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought near Lake Superior to begin the month. Rainfall totals up to around a half inch above normal were observed  across the county through the month. D1 Moderate Drought spread across the remainder of the county with no change in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 2nd. No additional changes in the drought status were observed through the remainder of the month despite the slightly above normal rainfall.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across the northwestern quarter of the county with D2 Severe Drought across the remainder of the county. Precipitation amounts of 1 to 2 inches over the first two weeks of the month led to the removal of the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 16th, leaving the entire county in D2 Severe Drought. Less than a half inch of precipitation was received over the remainder of the month and no additional changes in the drought status were observed.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across the eastern quarter of the northern part of the county with D2 Severe Drought across the remainder of the county. Precipitation amounts of 1 to 2 inches over the first two weeks of the month led to the removal of the area of D3 Extreme Drought with the update on the 16th, leaving the entirety of northern St. Louis County in D2 Severe Drought. Less than a half inch of precipitation was received over the remainder of the month and no additional changes in the drought status were observed.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the central part of the county. Precipitation amounts of 1 to 1.5 inches over the first two weeks of the month led to the trimming of the area of D2 Severe Drought in the far southeastern corner with the update on the 16th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought in this area. Only around a tenth of an inch of precipitation was received over the remainder of the month and no additional changes in the drought status were observed.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the northern part of the county. Precipitation was near to very slightly above normal for the month, but no changes in the drought status were observed.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the southern part of the county. Rainfall during the last week of October led to the removal of D2 Extreme Drought in areas along and south of the Mississippi River, being replaced with D1 Moderate Drought. Precipitation over the remainder of the month was near to very slightly above normal and no additional changes in the drought status were observed.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the northern part of the county. Rainfall during the last week of October led to the removal of D2 Extreme Drought in the southeastern half of the northern part of the county, being replaced with D1 Moderate Drought with the update on the 2nd. Precipitation over the remainder of the month was near to very slightly above normal with most of it falling during the first two weeks. This led to further reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 16th, leaving only areas along and north of US 2 in D2 Severe Drought with D1 Moderate Drought across the remainder of the northern part of the county. No additional changes in the drought status were seen over the remainder of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the far northeastern corner of the southern part of the county. Rainfall during the last week of October led to a slight reduction of D2 Extreme Drought, being replaced with D1 Moderate Drought. Precipitation over the remainder of the month was near to very slightly above normal with most of it occurring over the first two weeks of the month. With the update on the 16th, the remainder of the area of D2 Severe Drought was removed leaving D1 Moderate Drought and a tiny area of D0 Abnormally Dry in the far southern part of the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the northern quarter of the county. Rainfall during the last week of October led to the removal of D2 Extreme Drought across the county with the update on the 2nd, leaving a small area of D1 Moderate Drought in the north and D0 Abnormally Dry over much of the county.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of the northern part of the county. Rainfall during the last week of October led to the removal of D2 Extreme Drought for areas west of the Mississippi River with the update on the 2nd, leaving D2 Extreme Drought in areas along and east of the Mississippi River. Precipitation of 1 to 2 inches was observed over the month which was slightly above normal for most of the area. However, no additional changes in the drought status were observed over the remainder of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across most of southern St. Louis County along with the far northwest corner of Carlton County. D1 Moderate Drought was observed from the Twin Ports area into most of Carlton County. Precipitation of an inch to an inch and a half was received during the first two weeks of the month leading to a slight reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought in the southeastern corner of St. Louis County. An overall dry remainder of the month resulted in no additional changes to the drought index.

Most of the area was under D3 Extreme Drought conditions to begin the month outside of the eastern tip of Cook County which was in D2 Severe Drought. Slightly above normal precipitation thorugh the first few weeks of the month resulted in the reduction of D3 Extreme Drought across the western third of Lake County, being replaced with D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 16th. Additional precipitation over the remainder of the month on the order of 1 to 2 inches plus pushed the monthly total well above normal for most of the area except for far northern Lake County. Further reduction in the area of D3 Extreme Drought across the southern reaches of both Lake and Cook counties was seen with the update on the 30th.

Much of the area was under D2 Severe Drought with areas of D3 Extreme Drought across the northeastern tip of the county to begin the month. Several bouts of precipitation were seen through the first half of the month with heavier precipitation the last week of the month. This pushed precipitation totals for the month 1 to 2 inches plus above normal, especially across the eastern half of the area. This lead to the removal of D3 Extreme Drought in the region leaving D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 30th.
ASOS station KGNA at the Bay of Grand Marais recorded a peak gust of 62 mph at 4:41 PM CST. Winds gusted to 50 to 60 mph for about 3 hours during the late afternoon and early evening hours.

Much of the area was under D3 Extreme Drought with areas of D2 Severe Drought across the eastern tip of the county to begin the month. Several bouts of precipitation were seen through the first half of the month with heavier precipitation the last week of the month. This pushed precipitation totals for the month 1 to 2 inches plus above normal, especially across the eastern half of the area. This lead to the removal of D3 Extreme Drought in the region leaving D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 30th.
While most of the county received less than 6 inches of snow, the far southeastern corner of the county received 7 inches of snow from the storm.
Snowfall totals of 3 to 7 inches were reported across northern St. Louis County with a max report of 7.3 inches at a COOP site near Orr.

Snowfall totals of 10 to 15 inches were reported across the northern portions of Lake and Cook counties. The highest reports were from the southern part of the area where terrain effects led to enhanced snowfall with 18 inches reported 20 miles north of Grand Marais.
Snowfall of 6 to 12 inches was received across the northern portion of the county.
Snowfall of 6 to 12 inches was received across the central portion of St. Louis County. The highest reports were along the Iron Range with 15 inches reported near Chisholm being the highest.

Heavy snowfall was received in southern Lake County near Lake Superior with both terrain and lake enhancement effects occurring. Snowfall totals of 10 to 14 inches were reported with a high report of 16 near Finland.

Blizzard conditions lasting almost 12 hours were observed across southern Cook County along the North Shore of Lake Superior. In addition to the blizzard conditions, heavy snowfall blanketed the area in 14 to 18 inches of new snow with upwards of 20 inches just northwest of Grand Marais. Wind gusts near Grand Marais topped out in the 70 to 80 mph range for a period around 6 hours during the morning and mid-day hours. A max gust of 80.1 mph was recorded at 11AM 4 miles west of Grand Marais.
Widespread snowfall of 6 to 9 inches fell across northern Cass County with a high report of 10 inches at Cass Lake.
Widespread snowfall totals of 8 to 12 inches were reported across southern Itasca County with a high report of 12.7 inches near Cohasset.
Heavy snowfall fell across southern Cass County and over 6 inches had piled up near Pillager in about 5 hours. Storm totals of 4 to 8 inches were reported when snow ended.

Snowfall began earlier than expected across Crow Wing County and was heavier than expected as well. The Brainerd area reported 7 inches of accumulation after about 9 hours with totals of 6 to 10 inches by the time the snow ended later that evening.

Heavy snowfall was reported across southern St. Louis and Carlton counties during the storm with 7 inches reported in Rice Lake in less than 12 hours. Snowfall totals up to a foot were received when snow ended the next morning.
Snowfall totals across Douglas County were generally in the 4 to 6 inches range with 7.3 inches reported near Solon Springs.

Heavier snowfall of 6 to 10 inches was received over northern Bayfield County due in part to lake and terrain enhancement. The highest report was from the Bayfield Peninsula where 11.1 inches was recorded.
Snowfall was a bit lighter across Ashland County but the southern part of the county was able to accumulate 6 inches of snow by the time snow ended.
Heavier snowfall was observed over Iron County where lake and terrain enhancement combined to bring 6 to 10 inches of accumulation to much of the county.
Heavier than expected snowfall across Sawyer County brought widespread 6 to 9 inches across the area with 10 inches being reported near New Post.

Heavy snowfall brought upwards of 7 inches of accumulation to parts of the county in only 4 hours at the onset of the storm. Widespread totals of 8 to 10 inches were seen at the end of the event with a high report of 11 inches near Brantwood.
Heavy lake-effect snowfall led to widespread totals of 4 to 6 inches across southern Cook County with the highest report being 6.8 just west of Grand Marais.

Ashland County ended up on the northern edge of the system with most of the county receiving less that 6 inches of snow. However, the far southeastern corner did receive 6 to 7 inches of accumulation with a high report of 7.5 inches in Butternut.
Snowfall of 6 to 8 inches were common across Iron County with a high report of 9 inches along the border with Vilas County near Manitowish Waters.
Snowfall totals of 3 to 5 inches were common across Sawyer County with this system, but a locally intense area of snowfall led to a report of 10 inches near Stone Lake.
Price County received the most snow from this system with widespread reports of 8 to 12 inches. The highest report was 15.3 inches to the northwest of Phillips.
Snowfall of 6 inches in six hours was reported during the beginning of the storm with upwards of a foot received near Hovland by the time snow ended that evening.
Snowfall totals of 6 inches in six hours were recorded near Wascott during the morning of the 21st.
Snowfall of 6 inches in seven hours was reported to the northeast of Danbury on the 21st.
Just short of 8 inches of snowfall was measured in seven hours near Kerrick on the 21st.
Snowfall totals across the northern part of St. Louis County were generally under 6 inches being on the edge of the system, but the southwestern corner did reach 6 inches 12 hours after snow began.
Snowfall totals across Koochiching County were generally under 6 inches being on the edge of the system, but the southeastern corner did reach 6 inches 12 hours after snow began.
Reports from the northern portions of Lake and Cook counties were in the 5 to 8 inch range with reports of 6 to 12 inches closer to Lake Superior.
Snow totals over the northern portion of the county were in the 4 to 7 inch range with the highest report of 7 inches being recorded northwest of Bovey.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 7 inches were recorded across the central portion of the county with the highest reports occurring in the southern portion of the area.

Heavy snowfall and gusty winds led to blizzard conditions in areas of southern Lake County near Lake Superior. In addition to the blizzard conditions, snowfall totals of 7 to 12 inches were recorded with the highest report coming from Two Harbors with just over 13 inches.

Blizzard conditions persisted for around 6 hours during the morning of the 27th. Snowfall totals ranged generally from 4 to 9 inches but upwards of 17 inches were received on the hill just north of Grand Marais.
Snowfall totals of 4 to 8 inches were observed over the northern section of the county with the highest reports to the south.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were seen across southern Itasca County with multiple reports of 10 inches near Blackberry.
Widespread snowfall totals of 10 to 16 inches were seen across southern Cass County. The highest report was 18 inches near the community of Lake Shore.

Crow Wing County received some of the highest snowfall totals from this storm with much of the county receiving 10 to 16 inches. The highest total came from the far southwestern corner of the county near St. Mathias where 18 inches was measured.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were common around the county with the highest report being 10.8 inches near Palisade.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were common around the county with the highest report being 12 inches near McGrath.

Blizzard conditions lasting around 5 hours were seen in the Duluth area during the early morning hours of the 27th. In addition to the blizzard conditions, heavy snowfall also occurred with widespread reports of 6 to 10 inches. A few locations just to the northwest of Duluth received upwards of 11 inches of snow during the storm.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 12 inches were seen across the county with a few reports in excess of 13 inches. The highest total of 14 inches was reported in Finlayson.
Snowfall totals of 5 to 10 inches were reported across the county with the highest report of 13 inches coming from Lake Nebagamon.
Snowfall amounts of 6 to 10 inches were reported across the county with the highest report of 12.5 inches recorded near Sanborn.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were seen around the county with Mellen receiving 9.5 inches of snow when the storm ended.
Snowfall of 5 to 7 inches fell across Iron County with the Mercer area seeing around 8 inches of accumulation.

Heavy snowfall was observed across Burnett County with some areas receiving 6 inches of snow in four hours at the start of the event. Totals ranged from 6 to 11 inches with a few 12 inch reports in the Danbury, Siren and Webb Lake areas.
Total accumulations of 6 to 10 inches were observed around Washburn County with a report of 11.5 inches in Minong.
Widespread snowfall totals of 7 to 11 inches were received from around the county with a report of 14 inches just northwest of Winter.
Price County ended up on the southern edge of the storm with snowfall amounts ranging from 3 to 7 inches. The highest report of 8.8 inches was recorded near Park Falls.
Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were reported across the county with a high report of 10.3 inches on Rainy Lake east of International Falls.

Snowfall totals of 4 to 6 inches were observed across the northern part of the county, although higher totals were most likely received in far northern parts of the county which is wilderness area. The highest total received was 6.5 inches near Buyck.
Snowfall totals from the northern part of the county were in the 6 to 10 inch range with a max report of a foot about 16 miles north of Bovey.

An area of enhanced snowfall set up along the Iron Range during the event leading to totals of 5 to 7 inches with a high report of 8 inches near Celina. A two vehicle collision due to the ice and snow covered roads that occurred along Highway 1 west of Ely resulted in one fatality (indirect) and three serious injuries (indirect).
Heavy lake and terrain-enhanced snowfall fell across southern Lake County leading to totals of 8 to 12 inches. The highest report was 14 inches 10 miles north of Two Harbors.
Snowfall totals across southern Cook County were generally in the 3 to 5 inch range with a maximum report of 6 inches just east of Grand Marais.
Snowfall totals of 5 to 7 inches were reported across northern Cass County with high reports of 7 inches at both Cass Lake and Federal Dam.
Snowfall reports from the southern portion of Itasca County were in the 4 to 8 inch range with a high report of 9 inches in Grand Rapids.
Snowfall reports of 5 to 7 inches were received from the southern portion of Cass County with a high report of 8 inches near Lake Shore.
Snowfall totals across the county were generally under 6 inches, but a few 6 inch reports were received from the Brainerd area.

Snowfall totals of up to 5 inches were received from around the county, but some terrain-influenced heavier snowfall was observed along the Bayfield Peninsula to the northeast of the city of Bayfield.

No change in the drought conditions for Bayfield County this month. Conditions ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought across the Bayfield Peninsula to the Chequamegon Bay area. Rainfall totals were near the climatological average with slightly higher amounts along the northern coast but not enough to impact the drought status.

No change in the drought conditions for Ashland County this month. Drought conditions across Ashland County ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought near Chequamegon Bay. Rainfall totals were below average across the northern third of the county with above normal to the south.

No change in the drought conditions for Iron County. Drought conditions across Ashland County ranged from D0 Abnormally Dry over the far southern part of the county to D2 Severe Drought near Lake Superior. Rainfall totals were below average across the northern tip of the county with above normal to the south.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the county. Throughout the month the eastern portions of the county received precipitation of 1.5 to 2.25 inches above the normal. This led to a slight improvement along the east to D1 Moderate Drought by the end of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the northern part of the county. Throughout the month the region received precipitation of 0.75 to 2.25 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of most of the D2 Severe Drought from the area with the update on the 21st, leaving only the far northwestern corner which was removed on the 28th, leaving D1 Moderate Drought for the northern part of St. Louis County.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across most of central St. Louis County. Throughout the month the central portion of the county received precipitation of 1.5 to 3.0 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 21st leaving D1 Moderate Drought across the region.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across all of northern Itasca County. Throughout the month the majority of northern Itasca County received precipitation of 1.5 to 2.25 inches above normal, although the far northern portions of the county only received precipitation of 0.75-1.5 inches above normal. Most of the northern Itasca was upgraded to D1 Moderate Drought with the updated on the 21st and 28th, but the far northern portion still remains at D2 Severe Drought.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across areas along and north/east of the Mississippi River with D1 Moderate Drought south and west of the Mississippi. Throughout the month the southern portion of the county received precipitation of 1.5 to 3.0 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought with the updates on the 21st and 28th leaving a mix of D0 Abnormally Dry and D1 Moderate Drought across the area.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the far northern part of northern Cass County and D1 Moderate Drought across the remainder of northern Cass. Throughout the month the area received precipitation of 1.5 to 2.25 inches above the normal. However, the northern section only received 0.75 to 1.5 inches above normal.Despite this, the area of D2 Severe Drought was removed with the update on the 28th leaving a mix of D0 Abnormally Dry and D1 Moderate Drought across the area.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought for areas east of the Mississippi River in northern Aitkin County with the remainder of the county being in D1 Moderate Drought. Throughout the month the northern part of the county received precipitation of 1.5 to 3.0 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 21st leaving a mix of D0 Abnormally Dry and D1 Moderate Drought across the area.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across much of southern St. Louis County and the far northwestern corner of Carlton County with either D1 Moderate Drought or D0 Abnormally Dry across the remainder of the area. Throughout the month the area received precipitation of 0.75 to 2.25 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of D2 Severe Drought across the area with the update on the 21st leaving D0 Abnormally Dry or D1 Moderate Drought conditions in place.

The month began with D3 Extreme Drought across the northern portions of inland Lake and Cook counties with the remainder of th area in D2 Severe Drought. Throughout the month the area received precipitation of 0.75 to 2.25 inches above the normal. This led to the removal of D3 Extreme Drought and a slight reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought in western Lake County with the update on the 21st. No further improvements were seen over the remainder of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the eastern portions of the zone with the western half being at D1 Moderate Drought. Throughout the month the area received precipitation of 1.5 to 3.0 inches above the normal. This, however, had no impact on the drought status through the end of the month.

The month began with D2 Severe Drought across the entirety of southern Cook County. Throughout the month the area received precipitation of 0.75 to 2.25 inches above the normal. However, no improvement to the drought status was realized through the month.

Winds gusting to 40 mph across the county during the night of the 15th into the 16th resulted in widespread reports of trees snapped off and uprooted across the county leading to tree fires and power outages affecting over 500 customers along with blocked roads. At some point during the event, every fire department, ambulance service and law enforcement agency in the county responded to a call in the blowing snow and winds. No structures were damaged during the event. It is unknown if the tree damage occurred during the late evening thunderstorms or the gusty winds overnight.

Snowfall reports of 1 to 3 inches were reported across the county. Wind gusts of upwards of 40 mph led to blowing snow and visibilities reduced to under a half mile during the midday hours of the 16th that led to difficult travel conditions.

Snowfall reports of 1 to 3 inches were reported across the northern part of the county. Wind gusts of upwards of 35 mph led to blowing snow and visibilities reduced to under a half mile during the late morning hours of the 16th that led to difficult travel conditions.

Snowfall reports of 1 to 3 inches were reported across the county. Wind gusts of upwards of 35 mph led to blowing snow and visibilities reduced to under a half mile during the late morning hours of the 16th that led to difficult travel conditions.

Snowfall reports of 1 to 3 inches were reported across the county. Wind gusts of upwards of 45 mph led to blowing snow and visibilities reduced to under a half mile during the mid to late morning hours of the 16th that led to difficult travel conditions.
